Meet AMAA, Neri&Hu’s pick for the most influential architect of the next 20 years

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1411 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Photography by Mikael Olsson unless stated.
  • An innovative approach to the reuse of existing buildings defines the output of Italian architecture office AMAA, which Neri&Hu has selected as one of 20 names to watch in architecture and design as part of Dezeen’s 20×20 project, sponsored by Kohler.
  • Led by Marcello Galiotto and Alessandra Rampazzo, over the past 14 years AMAA has become known for its approach to the reuse of post-industrial structures in northern Italy, with the transformation of a former factory building into its own studio, a typical example of its approach.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Mikael Olsson unless stated.

An innovative approach to the reuse of existing buildings defines the output of Italian architecture office AMAA, which Neri&Hu has selected as one of 20 names to watch in architecture and design as part of Dezeen’s 20×20 project, sponsored by Kohler.

Led by Marcello Galiotto and Alessandra Rampazzo, over the past 14 years AMAA has become known for its approach to the reuse of post-industrial structures in northern Italy, with the transformation of a former factory building into its own studio, a typical example of its approach.

According to Galiotto, these buildings are a taste of what the studio wants to achieve.

“What we have done in the past 10 years is really just a sketch of what we can do in the future,” he told Dezeen.

“Our research is still growing, and it can be applied to various programmes and contexts,” he continued, “but in 20 years we will both be 60 so we want the studio to be able to evolve and grow in new directions.”.

The preservation and adaptation of existing buildings, which is central to AMAA’s practice, is a key reason why architects Lyndon Neri and Rossana Hu selected the studio for Dezeen’s 20×20 series.

“AMAA is significant for its fierce commitment to adaptive reuse,” remarked the duo, adding that the studio’s ability to repurpose historic structures “positions them as leaders in circular, life-cycle thinking in contemporary Italian architecture”.

AMAA is significant for its fierce commitment to adaptive reuse, [which] positions them as leaders in circular, life-cycle thinking in contemporary Italian architecture.

Galiotto and Rampazzo met Neri and Hu when they participated in the 2023 Venice Biennale and have since been invited to host lectures at the University of Pennsylvania, where Hu is chair of the architecture department.

“We have a long relationship with Lyndon and Rossana who we consider to be both amazing people and great architects so it’s truly an honour to be selected by them,” said Galiotto.

Rampazzo added that she saw a clear overlap between Shanghai-based Neri&Hu’s work, which also has a focus on adaptive reuse approach, and their approach at AMAA.

Sources indicate that “I’m a fan of their work and I see similarities in the way we do architecture and also the way we teach, despite our different cultural backgrounds,” she remarked. “I also love how they really support students and young architects by sharing their knowledge. We have a lot to learn from them but I hope we can have the same kind of legacy.”.

Rampazzo and Galiotto have known each other for more than 20 years after meeting while studying architecture at the Iuav University of Venice.

The studio now has offices in Venice and in the industrial town of Arzignano, and has gradually become established among Italy’s most respected architecture firms thanks to projects such as their own office and a cafe housed within a 19th-century town hall.

We felt our education hadn’t provide us with knowledge of how to run a medium or large-scale practice, so my experience with Sou Fujimoto was about closing the gap between the present and future of our studio.

The pair studied together at Iuav under the professorship of Massimo Carmassi, who they cite as an important influence on their approach to restoration and reuse.

After graduating in 2010, they assisted Carmassi and briefly set up a studio with friends to work on competitions. Then Galiotto went to Japan to work for Sou Fujimoto, while Rampazzo travelled to India for her PhD studies.

“We felt our education hadn’t provide us with knowledge of how to run a medium or large-scale practice,” said Galiotto, “so my experience with Sou Fujimoto was about closing the gap between the present and future of our studio.”.

This global travel and work experience helped open their minds to alternative approaches and opportunities, as well as giving them the confidence to set up their own studio back in Venice.

Sources indicate that “We’re still evolving, and evolving our identity,” stated Galiotto. “But the important thing was to find ourselves. That’s why the path was complicated.

“Stay in Italy… going outside of Italy… travelling the world as much as we can to see things. That was the key, I think, to the position that we are covering right now in the panorama of architecture in Italy.”.

In 2015, they opened a branch office in Galiotto’s hometown of Arzignano, which has been described as an “AMAA playground” due to the number of projects the practice has completed there.

Galiotto pointed out that their work in the town is part of an ongoing research into how architecture can blur the line between private and public spaces, with the Caffe Nazionale project providing a good example.

“Although the cafe is privately owned, it also forms the edge of a plaza so we wanted to give the space back to the people,” the architect explained, adding that the studio has coined the term “super public” to describe this aspect of their practice.

Alongside their work in Arzignano and Venice, AMAA now has commissions across Italy, including hospitality and residential projects, as well as schools and a theatre. Along with a focus on reuse, especially industrial buildings, Galiotto believes that the studio’s work is united by its considered eclecticism.

According to recent reports, “We’re influenced by art, artists, travels and whatever we can be – by curiosity,” he said. “I would say it’s something that’s very key and it gives us this kind of eclecticism. Our architecture in this moment is very eclectic and at the same time has a strong direction.”.

“It’s like a piano symphony, very complicated and very up and down, but at the same time very right like a poem, very well taught and very well executed, but very complicated in terms of ingredients.”.

The studio’s expanding list of projects has caused it to swell in size to approximately 30 members of staff, which Galiotto suggested is necessary to facilitate their detailed, research-led approach.

We often collaborate closely with other architects, but we are also influenced by painting, sculpture and photography which enhances the eclecticism of our projects.

Looking ahead, the architects said their main objective is to continue developing their team and consolidating their approach so that others can carry it on in the coming decades.

One concern they have is maintaining the same quality of output as demand for their services grows and they take on an increasing number of projects.

In just the past year they have completed 10 projects – as many as they delivered during the first decade of their practice – with public commissions now joining their work for private clients.

Despite the rapid growth, Galiotto and Rampazzo insisted their approach remains consistent whatever scale of project they are working on, whether it’s a chair, a public plaza or a museum, which they both agree would be a dream next project.

Asked for her view on the future of architecture over the coming decades, Rampazzo said there is a trend in Italy towards involving other creatives in the design process, which represents an alternative to the more autocratic approach of the past.

“Sharing ideas and opinions leads to more interesting outcomes,” she claimed. “We often collaborate closely with other architects, but we are also influenced by painting, sculpture and photography which enhances the eclecticism of our projects.”.

In their teaching roles at institutions including Kent State University and Universidade do Minho in Portugal, Galiotto and Rampazzo are responsible for helping to shape the attitudes of the next generation of architects, who they recognise are entering the workplace in challenging times.

Galiotto noted if there is one thing he tries to pass on to his students and the staff in his studio it is to “have passion and to keep pushing for what you believe in.”.

“If you are humble, passionate and curious then you can find success,” he added. “Sometimes it can be tough, but when you love what you do you can live your life feeling like you never worked for a single day.”.

Sources indicate that to celebrate Dezeen’s 20th birthday, we asked 20 of the most influential architects and designers of the last 20 years to identify someone they think will have a major impact in the next 20 years. Over the next four weeks, we’ll reveal their picks in a series of profile interviews.

Photography by Mikael Olsson unless stated.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The German government has agreed to hand over an extensive photo archive to the Jehovah’s Witnesses that documents the persecution of a pacifist Christian family under the Nazi regime.
  • Jehovah’s Witnesses were persecuted by the Nazis for their religious beliefs, particularly their refusal to serve in the military, pledge allegiance to Adolf Hitler, or participate in Nazi organizations.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The German government has agreed to hand over an extensive photo archive to the Jehovah’s Witnesses that documents the persecution of a pacifist Christian family under the Nazi regime.

Jehovah’s Witnesses were persecuted by the Nazis for their religious beliefs, particularly their refusal to serve in the military, pledge allegiance to Adolf Hitler, or participate in Nazi organizations. An estimated 4,500 Jehovah’s Witnesses were sent to concentration camps.

According to a report by The Latest York Times, among those persecuted were Franz and Hilda Kusserow and their 11 children, who lived in Bad Lippspringe, a town in the German state of North Rhine-Westphalia. Two of the couple’s sons were executed after refusing military service because of their religious beliefs. The three youngest children were taken from their family and placed in a Nazi training school, where they were prohibited from contacting their relatives. Both parents and their remaining children were sentenced to prison terms.

Industry observers note that one of their daughters Annemarie Kusserow was arrested by the Gestapo in October 1944 and remained a prisoner until May 25, 1945, after the war in Europe had ended. Over the following decades, Annemarie gathered and preserved a collection of more than 1,000 photographs, documents, drawings, letters, and reports documenting her family’s experiences.

Sources indicate that in her 2005 will, Annemarie bequeathed the entire photo archive to the German headquarters of the Jehovah’s Witnesses. However, her brother Hans Werner Kusserow, to whom she had loaned the collection for research purposes, sold it to the Bundeswehr Military History Museum in Dresden, Germany, in 2009. The archive has remained in the German museum’s possession ever since.

According to the Jehovah’s Witnesses’ official website, the sale of the photo collection to a military museum was “especially troubling” given that two of Annemarie’s brothers had lost their lives because of their pacifist beliefs. The organization notes the sale of the archive “resulted in years of legal battles.”.

Industry observers note that the Jehovah’s Witnesses filed a lawsuit to recover the archive from the Bundeswehr Military History Museum, which is operated by the German armed forces. On November 19, the museum and the religious organization reached an “amicable agreement” under which the collection will be handed over to the Jehovah’s Witnesses. Both parties have agreed to keep the terms of the settlement confidential.

According to The New York Times, Sebastian Stock, a spokesman for the religious organization in Germany, notes that once the transfer is complete, the “Jehovah’s Witnesses will develop and present a concept for making the archive accessible for further academic research.”.

In addition to digitizing the archive and making it available to scholars, the Jehovah’s Witnesses plan to display some of the documents in a fresh exhibition examining the history of the religious group in Central Europe.

Breaking: Mariana of Austria, royal art patron who saw power in portraiture, explored in Prado exhibition

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (738 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mariana of Austria’s position in the 17th-century Spanish court was not an easy one.
  • Industry observers note that the Museo Nacional del Prado in Madrid is taking a closer look at the Spanish monarch as it opens its first exhibition devoted to a female patron of the arts.
  • “The exhibition reveals a sovereign who was not simply the subject of some of the most celebrated portraits of the Spanish Golden Age, but who understood the political power of images and actively used them to assert and legitimise her authority,” says the exhibition curator Noelia García Pérez, a professor of art history at the Universidad de Murcia.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mariana of Austria’s position in the 17th-century Spanish court was not an easy one. She became queen of Spain in 1649 after marrying Philip IV, and then when he died in 1665, she assumed the role of regent, governing for over a decade on behalf of their three-year-old son, Charles II. Her authority was challenged, repeatedly. She was also the last woman of the Habsburg dynasty to exercise governing authority within the Spanish court. Even after her regent years were over, Mariana of Austria remained a significant figurehead until her death in 1696.

Industry observers note that the Museo Nacional del Prado in Madrid is taking a closer look at the Spanish monarch as it opens its first exhibition devoted to a female patron of the arts. Titled Mariana of Austria, the show reflects the museum’s efforts in recent years to re-examine historic women artists, benefactors and subjects. It includes around 100 objects, from paintings to prints and medals to manuscripts, building up a comprehensive picture of the iconography that Mariana used to curate her own public persona.

“The exhibition reveals a sovereign who was not simply the subject of some of the most celebrated portraits of the Spanish Golden Age, but who understood the political power of images and actively used them to assert and legitimise her authority,” says the exhibition curator Noelia García Pérez, a professor of art history at the Universidad de Murcia.

The Prado is poised to host such a presentation since it holds the most comprehensive collection of portraits of Mariana of Austria, representing every stage of her life from her youth as an Austrian archduchess up until her late years as queen mother. A full-length portrait of her by Diego Velázquez, within the Prado collection, was the model for her official image during the early years of her reign.

Frans Luycks, Infanta Mariana of Austria (around 1646)Museo Nacional del Prado.

In a recent development, mariana of Austria was in good company among other European royals who understood that authority needed a visual translation, to be communicated both domestically and across Europe. Some of the iconographic devices used by her court painters had precedents elsewhere, including among other queens. Such strategies include the use of the seated portrait, which was traditionally associated with ruling princes, and portraits in which she held a document as a reference to her governing ability.

In a recent development, preparation of the exhibition has led to both a different understanding of such iconography, and a deeper knowledge of the works themselves, thanks to restorations and a reassessment of dates, identifications and attributions of several works. The exhibition also reunites rarely seen and never before exhibited works, such as a double portrait of Mariana of Austria and Charles II, on loan from the Bečov nad Teplou Castle in the Czech Republic, and a bust attributed to Nicolás de Bussy, which was recently identified as a portrait of the queen.

Sources indicate that another section of the exhibition is devoted to portraits of queens, regents and other female governors who held power within the Spanish monarchy over the course of roughly two centuries. “Seeing these works together reveals how attributes such as the book and the column were passed down and acquired new meanings from one generation to the next,” Garcia Pérez says, “gradually shaping a shared visual language in which piety, dynastic legitimacy and the exercise of power were closely intertwined.”.

Mariana of Austria culminates a year of focusing on three queens at the Prado—Elisabeth Farnese, Christina of Sweden and now Mariana of Austria—exploring not only their tastes but also how they used the arts as a means of asserting their authority. This focus is part of the Prado’s commitment, over the past decade, to highlight the multifaceted roles of women in art history. These initiatives have evolved into the long-term programme called The Female Perspective, which will investigate the influence of Europe’s ruling women on the arts in collaboration with the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam.

It has been revealed that the next exhibition in the works will focus on female patrons of the 19th century, highlighting figures such as Spain’s Isabella II. “Ultimately, the ambition of The Female Perspective is not simply to add women’s names to an established narrative,” Garcia Pérez claims. “But to enrich and, where necessary, rethink that narrative.”.

• Mariana of Austria, Museo Nacional del Prado, Madrid, until 28 March 2027.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Built on a formerly disused site in Greenwich, the development contains 452 homes, all of which are social housing.
  • Construction company Durkan delivered Kidbrooke Park Road for the Royal Borough of Greenwich as part of its council housing programme, Greenwich Builds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Kilian O’Sullivan.

A collection of brick-clad buildings containing over 450 homes forms Kidbrooke Park Road in London, which architecture studio HTA Design claims is the largest upcoming-build council housing development in the UK.

Built on a formerly disused site in Greenwich, the development contains 452 homes, all of which are social housing.

Construction company Durkan delivered Kidbrooke Park Road for the Royal Borough of Greenwich as part of its council housing programme, Greenwich Builds.

HTA Design mentioned the project “demonstrates what can be achieved when local authorities take an ambitious approach to housing delivery”.

“Our main goal was to demonstrate that council housing delivered at scale does not have to come at the expense of good design,” HTA Design managing partner Simon Bayliss told Dezeen.

“We wanted to create a neighbourhood where the homes are generous and adaptable, where landscape is integral rather than an afterthought, and where streets and public spaces feel active, welcoming and safe,” he continued.

Recent findings suggest that “Together, the two phases have delivered the UK’s largest council housing development and one of the most significant social housing projects completed in recent years. We hope it serves as a benchmark for how future generations of affordable housing can be delivered across London and the UK.”.

HTA Design recently completed the second phase of the scheme, which adds eight housing blocks with 330 homes to the three blocks completed in phase one.

Ranging from six to 15 storeys, the housing comprises one-, two-, and three-bedroom apartments and family maisonettes, most of which are dual-aspect.

The buildings at Kidbrooke Park Road have a reinforced concrete frame, clad in brick chosen to reference red-brick buildings in the local area.

Arched entrances, patterned brickwork and exposed concrete elements were designed to add visual interest among the development’s green spaces, which include tree-lined streets, community gardens, wildflower meadows, play areas and gardens designed for rainwater runoff.

“A key challenge was ensuring that two phases delivered separately would ultimately come together as one place,” said Bayliss.

“Through simple buildings and typologies with repetitive architectural components, combined with a landscape strategy that runs throughout the development, we set out to create a neighbourhood with a clear identity that worked within its context.”.

According to recent reports, elsewhere in the development are a nursery, community facilities and green roofs. The housing is complete with air-source heat pumps, electric boilers and rooftop photovoltaics.

“We hope residents feel proud to live here,” Bayliss concluded.

“Beyond the homes themselves, the project has been designed to support everyday life, with play spaces, shared green areas, a nursery, community facilities and local amenities all contributing to a strong sense of community,” he remarked.

“Those are often the things that transform a housing development into a genuine neighbourhood.”.

The deputy mayor of London for Housing and Residential Development Tom Copley noted the project represents how London is “leading the way nationally on council home building”.

“The latest development at Kidbrooke Park Road is the perfect example of what we’re achieving, with 452 council homes forming the largest single entirely new-build council housing development in the country,” he stated.

“We recently revealed that 60 per cent of the funding from the first round of the mayor’s newly introduced Social and Affordable Homes Programme will go to London boroughs, and we look forward to that decision delivering even more new council homes in future.”.

Last month, the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) confirmed the brick-clad Lion Green Road housing by Mary Duggan Architects with Ruff Architects, which contains a mix of private and socially rented homes, as the winner of this year’s Stirling Prize.

RIBA also awarded its Neave Brown Award for Housing to Rowan Court, a cluster of brick-clad social housing blocks in Seven Sisters designed by Satish Jassal Architects.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Brightin Star first unveiled its fresh APO 35mm f/1.7 ASPH. lens for Leica M-Mount cameras at CP+ in February and then launched it on Kickstarter in August. As of today, it’s available to everyone, and it’s still as handsome as ever.

According to recent reports, the Brightin Star 35mm f/1.7 APO ASPH. is a full-frame, manual-focus lens with a native Leica M-Mount design. However, as evidenced by the fact that Brightin Star offers it in kits with E, Z, RF, X, L, and even GFX adapters, it’s easy to adapt to other camera systems. Although Brightin Star does not state the lens’s exact image circle when used with its GFX adapter, the tech giant says it covers the 44 x 33-millimeter sensor inside GFX system medium-format mirrorless cameras.

It has been revealed that although rangefinder-coupled with close focusing down to 0.7 meters (2.3 feet), the lens can focus as close as 0.3 meters (0.98 feet) when used in live view or adapted. Brightin Star notes that 100 degrees of focus throw covers infinity to 0.7 meters, while an additional 207 degrees covers the relatively narrow distance from 0.3 to 0.7 meters. That 307 degrees of total focus rotation is quite a lot, and Brightin Star describes it as “cinema style.”.

The 35mm f/1.7 prime is a compact, relatively lightweight lens. It measures just 43 millimeters (1.7 inches) long and weighs around 260 grams (9.2 ounces). It accepts 39mm front filters. Part of Brightin Star’s fresh “Apex” series of lenses, the 35mm f/1.7 APO ASPH. promises precision build quality and high-end optical performance.

Industry observers note that “We believe a truly exceptional M-mount lens should never have to choose between heritage and innovation,” Brightin Star says. “The Apex Series was created with this belief at its core. It preserves the timeless, understated character of classic M lenses while bringing together advanced optics, precision mechanics, and uncompromising standards of craftsmanship.”.

In a recent development, on the topic of image quality, the lens features 11 elements arranged across seven groups. There are some notable elements inside, including three double-sided aspherical lenses, three high-refractive pieces of glass, and an ED element. There are also two floating lens groups that move independently during focusing, which the manufacturer states better controls distance-related aberrations and reduces spherical aberrations at close range. The lens also promises minimized focus breathing.

As evidenced by the “APO” in its name, Brightin Star indicates this is an “apochromatic” lens. While there’s no precise, industry-standard definition for what level of performance that requires, Brightin Star promises minimal chromatic aberration. An apochromatic lens focuses red, blue, and green wavelengths of light at the exact same point on the image plane. The closer a lens gets to achieving this ideal, the fewer chromatic aberrations it exhibits, all else being equal.

Recent findings suggest that the Brightin Star MF 35mm f/1.7 APO ASPH. lens is available now for $1,099 for Leica M. An adapter adds $30, pushing the price to $1,129.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • From musicians and chefs to comedians, content creators are finding their performances copied by AI-generated characters that mimic their movements, jokes, and even the backgrounds in their original videos.
  • Recent findings suggest that the phenomenon, known as “reskinning,” is becoming increasingly common across social media thanks to cheap and accessible AI tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Content creators are increasingly discovering AI-generated versions of their videos in which almost everything is identical, except that they have been replaced by AI-generated characters.

From musicians and chefs to comedians, content creators are finding their performances copied by AI-generated characters that mimic their movements, jokes, and even the backgrounds in their original videos.

Recent findings suggest that the phenomenon, known as “reskinning,” is becoming increasingly common across social media thanks to cheap and accessible AI tools. People can take an existing video and replace the original performer with an artificial character, often designed to look funny, realistic, or hypersexualized.

The Instagram page More Perfect Union points to Higgsfield AI and its fresh Genjutsu tool that allows users to upload any video file and remix it with the user’s own character, locations, or product. However, other elements of the video remain untouched.

Just a few weeks ago, Nvidia invested in Higgsfield AI in a Series B funding round that raised $400 million. It gave Higgsfield a valuation of $5.4 billion.

A post shared by More Perfect Union (@perfectunion).

Recent findings suggest that sophie Lloyd, a U.K.-based guitarist who tours with U.S. rapper Machine Gun Kelly, tells the BBC she has spent years building an online following, only to see AI accounts reproduce content created by musicians and other performers.

“A lot [of these accounts] are getting thousands of views, thousands of followers, just for literally doing nothing and stealing the stuff that we’ve created,” Lloyd indicates.

Dr. Tina Kendall, an expert in online culture at Anglia Ruskin University, tells the British broadcaster that the practice is often less about experimentation with AI and more about exploiting content that has already demonstrated its popularity.

“What these tools allow people to do is just automatically take a viral concept that’s already existing and to reuse it through these reskinning tools,” she states.

While some accounts may use the technology for entertainment, Kendall says others are deliberately copying successful videos in the hope of attracting an audience and generating revenue.

Industry observers note that she sees the trend as part of a wider online “hustle culture,” in which accounts look to turn attention and engagement into money. That can mean directing followers toward subscription-based fan pages featuring adult content, promoting risky cryptocurrency products such as meme coins, or simply taking advantage of monetization features offered by social media platforms.

For the original creators, identifying and stopping the accounts responsible can be extremely difficult.

Alwyn Cruz, who has built a following on social media by exposing AI-generated musicians, describes trying to shut down these accounts as a game of whack-a-mole.

Industry observers note that “You don’t even know who’s making these [videos]. And then if you shut it down, they’re just going to create another,” he says.

Cruz notes the problem extends well beyond musicians, with performers from a variety of disciplines finding their work replicated.

“It’s not only guitarists that are being cloned: there are drummers, taekwondo players that are being cloned, and I’ve seen this all over the internet.”.

According to recent reports, the accessibility of AI reskinning tools like Higgsfield means the practice could become increasingly difficult to contain. Creators can spend years developing an online presence and refining a style that audiences recognize, only to find that the same performances can be reproduced with a different face and a few clicks.

And while the AI-generated versions may be attracting attention, the people behind the original performances are often left watching someone else benefit from their work.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Photography by Leandro Bulzzano, Ricardo Letona.
  • Local studio Estudio A-G has foregrounded a sculptural timber structural element while implementing bold colours for the renovation of a 1960s house in Mexico City.
  • Originally built in 1962 by Jaime Ortiz Monasterio, Casa Magnolia is located in the residential neighbourhood of San Ángel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Leandro Bulzzano, Ricardo Letona.

Local studio Estudio A-G has foregrounded a sculptural timber structural element while implementing bold colours for the renovation of a 1960s house in Mexico City.

Originally built in 1962 by Jaime Ortiz Monasterio, Casa Magnolia is located in the residential neighbourhood of San Ángel.

In a recent development, monasterio designed the home as a domestic library for his brother, who was an avid reader and book collector. Over the decades, the house was renovated multiple times, obscuring the home’s original character.

In 2025, Andrés Gutiérrez, head of Estudio A-G, was commissioned to reinterpret the interior of the 275-square-metre residence for new inhabitants, preserving the architectural qualities that made the original design unique.

“The restoration was extremely respectful of the house’s original architecture, but we never wanted the result to feel nostalgic,” Gutiérrez told Dezeen.

“Quite the opposite – once restored, the house needed to feel completely fresh, fresh and contemporary, which was exactly what the clients were looking for.”.

Recent findings suggest that completed in February 2026, the design uses colour to achieve the transformation, bringing new energy to the original architecture without competing with it. The studio aimed to have the house be recognisably Mexican without falling into tropes.

“I wanted the house to feel unmistakably Mexican, but without relying on folklore or the usual clichés associated with ‘Mexican interiors’.” he remarked.

“I was much more interested in expressing that identity through materials, craftsmanship, colour and contemporary Mexican design.”.

At the centre of the house, a dark-toned timber structure rises through a series of split levels like a sculptural tree connecting the entrance hall, living room, dining room, study and reading areas before unfolding into a double-height ceiling.

“More than a structural element, it serves as a spatial anchor, establishing continuity throughout the interior and reinforcing the vertical dimension of the house,” Gutiérrez stated, explaining that wood acts as a warm, unifying element throughout the house.

The studio restored and reintegrated the original wood flooring, ceiling finishes and structural elements. It also reinstalled most of the original wooden bookshelves that had been dismantled and stored.

“Overall, the intervention focused on restoring the elements that were worth preserving while introducing the necessary contemporary updates to make the house fully functional for the way its new owners live today,” he said.

The studio replaced some window frames and all the glass, updated the lighting and electrical systems and rebuilt the bathrooms and kitchen.

However, one of the most significant interventions were the colour blocks and new materials included in the space.

“Colour plays a central role in the project,” Gutiérrez remarked, calling out soft blue walls that are a backdrop for deep plum sofas, moss green dining chairs, lilac rugs, green serpentine stone and terracotta-toned marble.

“Rather than acting as decoration, colour is used as an architectural tool to organise space, establish hierarchy, and shape atmosphere.”.

It has been revealed that he also designed custom furniture that pairs with historic pieces – like Antonio Attolini’s 1969 armchairs – and contemporary Mexican art. Works by Cecilia Barreto, Francisco Muñoz, Jorge Rosano, Daniel Berman and Adriana Silva embed culture into everyday life.

Previously, Estudio A-G designed a rooftop bar as a “matriarchal universe,” complete with crocodile-shaped furniture and shrine-like water, for a boutique hotel in a former Spanish colonial manor house in San Miguel de Allende.

In a recent development, tate Liverpool will reopen next autumn following an extensive four-year redevelopment costing around £30m. The relaunch programme includes a major show dedicated to Surrealism along with the first major retrospective for the Liverpool-based artist Chila Kumari Singh Burman. The key regional UK gallery, located on the city’s Royal Albert Dock, closed in October 2023 and was initially due to reopen in 2025.

Chila Kumari Singh Burman in front of her Winter Commission covering the façade of Tate Britain in London in 2020.

Surrealism: Staging Dream Worlds, which will run until spring 2028, will include work by Salvador Dalí, Eileen Agar and Man Ray, among others. “The show will reveal the vital role of Surrealism in the history of theatre and dance, from experiments with masquerade, character and role play to major commissions for stage sets and costumes,” notes a Tate statement. Works featured include Claude Cahun's photograph of Sheila Legge’s 1936 performance Surrealist Phantom of Sex Appeal, when the artist wore a Dalí-inspired costume in London's Trafalgar Square.

Claude Cahun, Sheila Legge as Surrealist ‘Phantom’, Trafalgar Square (1936).

© Claude Cahun; Image courtesy Jersey Heritage Collections.

For the overhaul, Tate Liverpool received £18.6m from the Public Bodies Infrastructure Fund, which is awarded by the UK Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport. It also received philanthropic donations from the Garfield Weston Foundation (£3m), the Wolfson Foundation (£1.25m) and the Ross Warburton Charitable Trust, alongside other trusts and individuals.

Sources indicate that the UK Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government also awarded £10m to the gallery, which it secured through a combined £20m bid with National Museums Liverpool. “We have raised more [than £30m] because there are other costs associated with reinstalling and reopening the museum,” a Tate spokesperson tells The Art Newspaper.

According to a Tate statement, the designs for the fresh gallery, drawn up by 6a architects, “open up spaces to display the incredible variety of Tate’s collection and host world-class exhibitions. These galleries will sit alongside new public spaces for play, relaxation and learning with views across the Mersey, helping to connect the gallery with the city and the communities that surround it.” The New York and Berlin-based artist Asad Raza will create the first major commission for the gallery’s Art Hall.

Tate Liverpool, which opened in 1988, was designed by James Stirling who converted the northwest corner of a seven-story warehouse standing on the Royal Albert Dock into the five-storey gallery. It received 405,000 visitors in 2022, its last full year, and 660,000 in 2019, before the Covid-19 pandemic.

It has been revealed that helen Legg stepped down as Tate Liverpool director earlier this year, with Jemima Pyne taking over in the interim; a fresh director will be recruited after the new director of Tate, Jessica Morgan, is in post next year, the spokesperson confirmed. Tate comprises four galleries: Tate Modern, Tate Britain, Tate Liverpool and Tate St Ives.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A family photographer has been arrested for allegedly hiding income from her photography business to obtain more than $30,000 in food assistance benefits.

Mary Miller, a 31-year-old Wisconsin-based family photographer who operated under the name Fawn Focus Photography, is facing multiple charges related to public assistance fraud.

According to a long-term investigation by the Dodge County Sheriff’s Office in Juneau, Wisconsin, Miller allegedly failed to report her earnings as a self-employed photographer while claiming FoodShare and childcare assistance benefits over several years. FoodShare is Wisconsin’s food assistance program for individuals and families with limited incomes.

According to a report by Fox 11 News, an investigation was launched after Dodge County Economic Support uncovered apparent inconsistencies between Miller’s tax records, employment records, court documents, and applications for public assistance.

Authorities allege that the photographer provided inaccurate information about her income and residency when applying for benefits, including failing to disclose earnings from her business Fawn Focus Photography.

Between 2019 and 2025, Miller allegedly received more than $30,000 in FoodShare benefits that she was not entitled to claim. She also received more than $22,000 in childcare assistance benefits, although investigators were still determining how much of that funding was improperly obtained.

According to online court records, Miller faces six counts of failing to disclose an event affecting her eligibility for benefits and six counts of failing to report the receipt of income or assets. The photographer made her initial court appearance this month and was issued a $5,000 signature bond.

“Public assistance programs exist to help individuals and families during times of genuine need and are funded by hardworking taxpayers,” Dodge County Sheriff Dale J. Schmidt tells Fox 11 News in a statement. “When someone is alleged to have concealed income or provided false information in order to obtain benefits, it undermines public trust and diverts limited resources away from those who legitimately qualify for assistance.”.

Previously, PetaPixel reported on a photographer who was sentenced to five years in federal prison for defrauding a family out of $4.6 million and using $200,000 of the money to purchase Taylor Swift concert tickets. 46-year-old photographer Chanise Coyne was given jail time after pleading guilty to wire fraud over a multimillion-dollar fraud scheme involving fictional child modeling events.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has now been five straight quarters of growth for the transformed, resurgent Eastman Kodak.

After facing immense financial challenges for decades, including warnings about its ability to continue as a “going concern” last year, Eastman Kodak has risen from the ashes like a phoenix, cashing in on analog’s revival.

According to recent reports, the star of the show for the Rochester, Fresh York-based Kodak is its Advanced Materials and Chemicals (AM&C) division, which posted 21% revenue growth in Q3 2026 compared to Q3 2025. While AM&C’s $99 million in revenue is significantly less than Kodak’s $165 million in Print revenue, the Print division’s revenue actually dipped 7% year-over-year. In total, Kodak’s consolidated revenues of $276 million this past quarter are up 3%. Profits are up, too, increasing by 7%.

“Kodak delivered strong performance in the third quarter, once again achieving year-over-year improvement in revenue, gross profit and Operational EBITDA,” claims Jim Continenza, Kodak’s Executive Chairman and CEO, in SEC filings.

According to recent reports, “We continue to execute our long-term blueprint and are seeing a return on our ongoing investments. Our primary growth engine, AM&C, is now our fastest-growing, most profitable unit. Our print business has performed well for the year to date despite challenging economic conditions. And, most importantly, we generated $27 million in cash for Q3, an crucial indicator of the operational strength of our business. Looking forward, we’re focused on continuing to invest in our core businesses and finishing the year with profitable growth,” Continenza continues.

It has been revealed that as Continenza says, AM&C is Eastman Kodak’s fastest-growing and most profitable business unit. What exactly is AM&C, though? Kodak says AM&C covers the manufacturing of still, motion picture, and industrial films, plus specialty chemicals related to film, technologies, and medicine.

As CineD reports, in a call with investors, Continenza specifically called out the growing desire among Hollywood filmmakers to shoot their biggest projects on film.

“Film continues to be the capture medium of choice for major features,” Continenza told investors.

While Christopher Nolan’s record-breaking IMAX epic, The Odyssey, made a lot of headlines for its use of over two million feet of film, it is just one example of the return of film to Hollywood. Kodak had a great story about The Odyssey in August that dug a bit deeper into the movie’s use of Kodak film.

Kodak says award-winning cinematographer and Director of Photography Hoyte van Hoytema used Kodak Vision3 250D 5207 for daytime exteriors and bright interiors, and Kodak Vision3 500T 5219 for low-light and night scenes.

It has been revealed that “The 250D and 500T are my sweet spot filmstocks. I love their grain structures and they’re very much my functional workhorses. The way I work with lenses, NDs, daylight and lights for night scenes, falls within the sensitivity curves of both those stocks. They are both versatile too. For example, I can shoot a little bit longer into magic hour with the 250D and I don’t have to resort too rapidly into going higher-up in ASA,” van Hoytema told Kodak.

Earlier this year, Kodak celebrated seven movies shot on Kodak that competed for the Palme d’Or at Cannes 2026, and the legendary film company routinely updates its list of productions shot on film.

Paper Tiger, Disclosure Day, and Marty Supreme are just a few big names on the list. Continenza also mentioned Sense and Sensibility and Digger in his call.

Then, of course, there’s Eastman Kodak’s growing still film business. Over the past year-plus, Eastman Kodak has brought photographic film sales back under its purview, rebranding many different stocks and even unveiling some newly introduced, albeit familiar, ones. The company reintroduced some larger-format photo film stocks a few months ago, too.

Between Hollywood’s reignited love affair with film and Eastman Kodak’s investment in both motion picture and still film production, it’s immediately evident that Eastman Kodak believes its path to future success goes through analog. The licensing deals for smash hit Kodak-branded products don’t hurt, either.

Industry observers note that muholi was born in 1972 in Umlazi, Durban, South Africa and lives today in Cape Town. They are a self-described visual activist, who, since the mid-2000s, have used photography to document the lives of LGBTQ+ people, initially in South Africa, where they were born.

Zanele Muholi, Diana Cristina Nascimento Ramos, Salvador, 2025, from Faces and Phases, ed. by Renée Mussai (MACK, 2026).

Courtesy of the artist and MACK.

They have since expanded their project around the world and work in discrete, often ongoing series that have a common aim: to respond to violence and discrimination against queer and trans communities, to reflect their defiance and resistance, and to expand their visibility in visual culture in South Africa in particular but also far beyond.

It has been revealed that zanele Muholi, Ashara Ekundayo, Venice, 2026, from Faces and Phases, ed. by Renée Mussai (MACK, 2026).

Courtesy of the artist and MACK.

In a recent development, the people they depict have, since the start, been far more than sitters or subjects; they are collaborators, participants who help define the way they are represented. A crucial factor is that Muholi turns the lens onto themself. “When I position myself in my own frame,” they have noted. “I do so on my own terms attempting to articulate my own way of seeing and wanting to be seen.”.

It has been revealed that zanele Muholi, Christine Madonsela, Daveyton, Gauteng, 2017, from Faces and Phases, ed. by Renée Mussai (MACK, 2026).

Courtesy of the artist and MACK.

And whether it is their unflinching and tender portraits of their collaborators or their imaginative and improvised self-portraits Muholi’s photographs are always beautiful objects, with a fastidious attention to the properties and possibilities of their medium.

Zanele Muholi, Mantedieng ‘Mantis’ Mamabolo-Cunningham, Parktown, Johannesburg, 2018, from Faces and Phases, ed. by Renée Mussai (MACK, 2026).

Courtesy of the artist and MACK.

They discuss the influence of their mother, who was a maker herself, and was a profound influence on one of their most notable works, Somnyama Ngonyama (2012). They reflect on the enormous impact of photographers including Rotimi Fani-Kayode, Lola Flash and Joan E. Biren, writers including Audre Lorde, and musicians including Brenda Fassie. Plus, they answer our usual questions, giving insight into their daily practices and the rhythms of their work, and reflecting on the ultimate question: what is art for?

Otherway reworks The Whisky Exchange brand identity around a lighter twin-lion crest, vibrant purple, and layered print full of discovery.

Industry observers note that the lions come first. Otherway kept the twin-lion crest at the heart of the brand and redrew it lighter and more fluid, so a heraldic mark that could have felt ceremonial now feels loose and alive. Around it, the whole system runs on one bold decision: a vibrant purple that holds everything together, a clear break from the dark greens and browns fine spirits usually hide behind. A major flared serif carries the line WHERE CURIOSITY KNOWS NO BOUNDS across the posters, while tasting cards stack in layers of orange, pink, blue and deep purple, borrowing the stamped edges and layered print of the labels themselves.

Sources indicate that type does the talking in three distinct voices. The headline serif is set huge, its flared strokes and sharp terminals giving even a single line the weight of a poster. The tasting cards switch to a small mono face, all even capitals, for the practical information: dates, prices, and flavour notes that read GINGER, APRICOT, ROSEMARY, COFFEE, GRAPE down the card. The manifesto panel drops to a plain sans on periwinkle blue, set as one calm block of copy. The grid behind it all is the stack itself. Cards overlap like printed labels, their scalloped edges and offset corners doing the work a border would do, and the Staff Picks poster splits its wordmark top and bottom around a single bottle, dead center.

In a recent development, the system proves itself on real surfaces. The lions leave the page as a gold blade sign, hung on the stone shopfront, and the same mark sits in deep purple at the top of the window vinyl. FINE SPIRITS from EVERY CORNER of the GLOBE runs down the glass in the same flared serif, with the shop's own line beneath it. Stamps and label textures layer across the cards and posters, and the identity carries through from bags to store, every detail considered, as rich and varied as the spirits themselves.

Mason & Fifth's Belsize Park guesthouse was designed to be “domestic and low-impact”

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Design studio Holloway Li has collaborated with architecture practice Latest-works to conceive the interiors of this London apartment hotel, incorporating circular features meant to stand the test of time.
  • Mason & Fifth guesthouses are composed of fully furnished private apartments where guests have the flexibility of staying anywhere from one night to several months at a time.
  • The company has three sites across London, with one in Primrose Hill, another in Westbourne Park, and now Belsize Park.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography courtesy of Mason & Fifth.

Design studio Holloway Li has collaborated with architecture practice Latest-works to conceive the interiors of this London apartment hotel, incorporating circular features meant to stand the test of time.

Mason & Fifth guesthouses are composed of fully furnished private apartments where guests have the flexibility of staying anywhere from one night to several months at a time.

The company has three sites across London, with one in Primrose Hill, another in Westbourne Park, and now Belsize Park.

The Belsize Park location occupies Ornan Court, a 19th-century mansion block that once formed part of the Ivy Bank residential estate.

Architecture practice Upcoming-works adapted the building for hospitality use, establishing a series of communal spaces at ground level that could serve as a social hub for guests.

At its heart is a large shared kitchen, centred by a chunky tiled breakfast island, followed by a lounge area with intimate groupings of timber-frame chairs and two khaki-coloured sofas, complementing the glossy green fireplace.

Recent findings suggest that just off this space is a cosy snug that’s been painted a warm ochre hue. It’s separated from the lounge by a custom-made curtain that design studio House of Quinn made from earth-toned fabric offcuts.

Holloway Li is behind the design of the interiors. Instead of doing a through-and-through overhaul, the studio instead aimed to develop a “circular economy aesthetic that felt warm, domestic and low-impact”.

“That ambition aligned with Mason & Fifth’s own sustainability agenda and allowed us to explore how historic buildings like this can be retrofitted in imaginative and progressive ways,” said the studio’s creative director Alex Holloway.

In each of the guesthouse’s 56 apartments, the bedrooms are furnished with demountable wardrobes in lieu of fitted joinery.

The wardrobes are made up of lightweight timber parts fixed together with metal brackets rather than glue so that, if necessary, they can be unassembled, flat packed, and re-built elsewhere.

Holloway Li worked with Marble Collective to create countertops and splashbacks for the apartment kitchens; all are crafted from limestone that’s been rejected from quarries because of inconsistencies.

The top edge of the splashbacks has been left slightly craggy and unfinished, further celebrating the stone’s natural flaws.

Almost all of the walls throughout the guesthouse have been simply rendered with multi-finish plaster, and any surface imperfections have been left on show.

“In many cases, the most sustainable decision is restraint,” explained Holloway Li’s senior designer Carrie Coningsby.

“Drawing on principles akin to kintsugi and spolia, the approach celebrates intervention rather than concealing it, embedding repair into the visual language of the space,” she added, referencing historic practices focused on reuse and repair instead of replacement.

Mason & Fifth Belsize Park was shortlisted in the sustainable interior category of this year’s Dezeen Awards.

Other projects in the running included the winning Cloudhaus Hotel by RooMoo, which is outfitted with materials salvaged from abandoned mountain cabins, and the London Coffee Factory by Steve Jensen Design, which is structured around a reclaimed timber framework.

Photography courtesy of Mason & Fifth.

Industry News: It took designers 20 years to bring this font back from the dead

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (398 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Creativebloq

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Paris-based foundry Production Type has revived the classic French typeface Vendôme, restoring it to its former glory.
  • In its early days, Vendôme was one of the best serif fonts – a celebration of France's post-WWII creative boom.
  • It has been revealed that vendôme first made its debut back in 1950, drawn by sculptor and set designer François Ganeau, with meticulous art direction from Roger Excoffon.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Paris-based foundry Production Type has revived the classic French typeface Vendôme, restoring it to its former glory. Once tainted by poor handwritten recreations and clunky scans, the font eventually lost its lustre, but with patience and craft, Production Type has revitalised this classic for the better.

In its early days, Vendôme was one of the best serif fonts – a celebration of France's post-WWII creative boom. Making a playful, contemporary debut, the newly introduced Vendôme Nouveau is a love letter to French heritage, with a elegant, modern refinement.

It has been revealed that vendôme first made its debut back in 1950, drawn by sculptor and set designer François Ganeau, with meticulous art direction from Roger Excoffon. Defined by its "leaning stems, wavering strokes, plunging Vs, and abruptly sharp serifs," the typeface became an icon of design, featuring on ads, book jackets, record sleeves, and film posters.

But the legendary font soon began to suffer from its own success, being recreated by sign painters and shopkeepers who wanted a slice of its fame. With the rise of phototypesetting, the font was endlessly copied, and by the 90s, the iconic typeface had countless iterations with varying degrees of quality and style.

Refusing to let the icon die, the Production Type team (and type historian PhDs) set about restoring the font to its former glory. A labour of love, the process took over 20 years of meticulous redrawing, using an array of archival paper proofs and filling the gaps of missing weights from scratch.

The font made an unconventional and wonderfully contemporary debut on the NYC subway, where commuters were snapped reading fake typographic self-help books like “How to Raise a Sans Serif in an All-Serif Family”.

Discover more about the project or take a look at the most iconic typefaces ever made.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A touchscreen MacBook has been on the wishlist of many Mac owners (and media commentators) for years, and now it’s finally here.
  • Industry observers note that why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you.
  • Recent findings suggest that there's a lot of ‘pro’ in this laptop.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A touchscreen MacBook has been on the wishlist of many Mac owners (and media commentators) for years, and now it’s finally here. While Apple hasn’t gone all the way and produced a 2-in-1 MacBook with a stylus, there are some applications for the touchscreen tech in creative apps, and the switch to OLED means there's incredible brightness on offer. The major drawback is that it’s even more expensive, especially as it only comes on top-end machines, but one day every MacBook might be like this.

Expensive, expensive, expensive.

Force Touch trackpad not immediately intuitive.

Industry observers note that why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

Recent findings suggest that there's a lot of ‘pro’ in this laptop. It’s a MacBook Pro. It has an M5 Pro CPU inside it. And it has Apple’s new PROLED XDR screen, which is a touchscreen OLED to everyone else. Is there any way that more pro-ness could have been squeezed in? Perhaps one of the Radeon Pro GPUs that graced the ‘Darth Vader’s dustbin’ generation of the Mac Pro?

Industry observers note that that aside, we might be looking at the future of the MacBook line. While for now the new screen is only available on a few top-end models, the benefits it brings - not only improved brightness but a thinner and lighter chassis - are likely to trickle down through the range.

Industry observers note that the MacBook Pro remains pro-fessional, has a powerful pro-cessor, and Apple’s hardware pro-wess means we shouldn’t get any pro-blems from the PROLED display. Let’s see. It could be heading to the top of our best laptop for animation guide.

3x Thunderbolt 5, 1x HDMI 2.1, 3.5mm audio.

• Slightly slimmer than before• Not a 2-in-1.

It has been revealed that first things first, the PROLED screen makes the 16in MacBook Pro a little slimmer and lighter. It’s also a stunner in terms of colour and brightness, but Apple is so late to this party it’s a little hard to get overexcited. We’ve had OLED touchscreens on Windows PCs since at least 2016 and Lenovo’s Yoga 14, and while the display tech is magnificent it does mean you end up with fingermarks all over your screen, especially if you’re using it after lunch.

According to recent reports, then there's the debate about what touchscreen laptops are actually for. In 2-in-1 designs you can bend the screen back and whip out a stylus for some sketching, but in a traditional laptop you’re more likely to use it for zooming and scrolling. Apple’s announcement event for the laptop showed someone using the touchscreen to play piano keys directly on its screen, and while this somehow seems unlikely, as surely your hands will be in entirely the wrong position, it can also be used to click and drag files, audio tracks, and to do a little precision brushwork with your fingertip if you need to. Happily, it’s optional, and the MacBook trackpad is as good as ever. The touchscreen supports most trackpad gestures, if you’re the sort to let their fingers dance, and as ever you can pay extra for the Nanotexture coating that cuts reflections.

Elsewhere, you get the usual MacBook Pro build. They’re really well made, and this one’s no exception. The switch to OLED has allowed for a millimetre to be shaved off the laptop’s thickness, and a few hundred grams to be shed from its weight. The weight reduction is the more noticeable of the two, making Apple’s largest laptop a touch more portable. By far the most important thing, however, is that the Apple logo on the MacBook’s lid once again lights up when the laptop is in use, and it’s the right way up.

• Thunderbolt 5• Excellent colour reproduction.

There are three Thunderbolt 5 ports on the MacBook Pro 16, all of which are compatible with USB4 peripherals, and as there's a full-size HDMI 2.1 port and a MagSafe 3 for charging, you won’t have to bog them down connecting to monitors and chargers. This opens them up for use with external SSDs, and given the extra cost of upgrading the storage in a modern Mac when you order, one of those will probably be on your shopping list.

The screen is the big latest feature for this 2026 release of the MacBook Pro 16, and this new OLED is an absolute beauty. It’s a ‘tandem’ OLED, which stacks two light-emitting layers on top of one another for a brightness boost, and it shows: Apple promises up to 2,000 nits of brightness if you feed it HDR content, a figure that rivals even its immensely bright Studio Display XDR. Colour is excellent too though you’ll need to manually activate the PROLED XDR P3 + AdobeRGB colour profile in the Settings app to get the most out of it. Do this, and you can expect 93% of Adobe RGB and 94% of DCI-P3 alongside 100% of sRGB.

According to recent reports, apple has also fiddled with the MacBook Pro’s hinge for a better touchscreen experience. Push too hard and you can find a laptop’s screen leaning away from you, but the hinge on the PROLED is noticeably stiffer than that on a non-touch MacBook. It’s also incredibly smooth, almost like there's some sort of hydraulic aspect to it, as it moves up and down.

On the front you’ll find Apple’s usual keyboard, which is pretty good, and a Force Touch trackpad that can take a bit of getting used to, especially if you’re used to holding the pad in to drag files about. This can trigger a deeper click that brings up file information, which is less useful than you might think, but it doesn’t take long to get the hang of, and you can change what it does in the settings.

In a recent development, we test every one of our laptops using the same benchmarking software suite to give you a thorough overview of its suitability for creatives of all disciplines and levels. This includes:.

It has been revealed that • Geekbench: Tests the CPU for single-core and multi-core power, and the GPU for the system's potential for gaming, image processing, or video editing. Geekbench AI tests the CPU and GPU on a variety of AI-powered and AI-boosted tasks.• Cinebench: Tests the CPU and GPU's ability to run Cinema 4D and Redshift.• UL Procyon: Uses UL Solutions' Procyon software suite to test the system's ability for AI image generation in Stable Diffusion, its Microsoft Office performance and its battery life in a looping video test.• Topaz Video AI: We use Topaz Video AI to test the system's ability to upscale video and convert video to slow-motion.• PugetBench for Creators: We use the PugetBench for Creators benchmarking suite to test the system's ability to run several key tasks in Photoshop and Adobe Premiere Pro, as well as its performance when encoding/transcoding video.• ON1 Resize AI: Tests the system's ability to resize 5 photos to 200% in a batch process. We take the total time taken to resize the images and divide by 5.

• Very fast CPU• GPU can't beat descrete chips.

Sources indicate that the PROLED MacBook is a premium product, and so comes with a choice of premium processors (and a premium price, but more on that later). It can be fitted with an M5 Pro, which is what we’ve got here, or an M5 Max that piles on the processing cores. There's no option for anything else, so you won’t be picking one up with a vanilla M5 in it. The M5 Pro and Max both use Apple’s Fusion Architecture to weld CPU dies together into one mega-chip, and the core counts make it look very much like the Pro is two normal M5s stuck together, with two cores disabled. It’s split into six Super cores and 12 Performance cores - the old Efficient cores are missing from this generation - and it can turbo up to 4.6 GHz.

Apple’s claim that the M5 offers the fastest single-core performance out there remains unbeaten in our tests. In the Geekbench 6 single-core test, the M5 Pro comes within a hair’s breadth of the M5 Max in a Mac Studio, a remarkable feat for a laptop. The Studio pulls ahead a bit in the multi-core test due to having more cores, but the Pro is right up there, actually beating the M5 Max from when we tested it in a MacBook Pro and leaving the M4 Pro behind.

Recent findings suggest that the fastest non-Apple single-core result in our tests, the Asus Zenbook A16 powered by a Qualcomm Snapdragon X2 Elite, now rests in tenth place in the Geekbench charts, and you have to go to 13th place before you find an X86 CPU, which is in a desktop gaming PC. Apple is completely dominant in this arena at the moment, and it’s only when you switch to the GPU test results that the gaming PCs rise to the top and the Apple chips get some real competition.

In real-world applications, the M5 Pro isn’t as fast at doing tasks such as denoising raw files in Adobe Camera Raw as an Nvidia GPU, but it’s way faster than trying to do it using the integrated graphics on most Intel or AMD chips.

The battery life of all the M5 generation MacBooks has been exceptional, but the OLED screen has tipped the 16in Pro over the edge into a machine that can be relied on for two whole days of use. Testing how long it could play a video until exhausted took a lot longer than on most other laptops, with a final figure in excess of 21 hours. Push it really hard and that will come down, of course, but it’s a remarkable achievement nonetheless.

Sources indicate that this is the thing that’s going to keep these first touchscreen Macs out of the hands of many creatives. The 16in model we’ve got here starts at £3,399 for one with 24GB of RAM and 1TB of storage, and just climbs and climbs as you add more stuff to it. You want 64GB of RAM and 4TB of storage? You can have it, but it’ll cost you £5,899 and you can go higher than that if you switch to the M5 Max. The touchscreen is a premium feature, and the same laptop with the old display starts from £2,999. The old M5 model no longer seems to be available, probably to make way for an M6, which is already there on the 14in version.

The fact this laptop even exists means Apple thinks there's a market for it, and if you’re a touchscreen laptop lover it may be the machine you’ve been dreaming of. There's no denying the expense, however, which means you’re really going to have to love it to consider it over other, better-value, choices.

Thinner and lighter than before.

Excellent CPU performance, GPU can't fight Nvidia.

Closer in performance to the MacBook Pro than to the MacBook Neo, the M5 edition of the MacBook Air is the bargain in Apple's range.

The frist generation of Nvidia's RTX Spark hardware looks promising for creatives. This 14-incher from Asus is powerful, well built, beautifully thin and light, and will last all day on a charge.

A mighty gaming laptop with a powerful GPU can make a good buy for a video editor or designer who likes to work on complex documents. This one from HP is slightly more subtly designed than many, and though its battery life is short it can surely speed up your workflows.

Sources indicate that ian Evenden has been a journalist for over 20 years, starting in the days of QuarkXpress 4 and Photoshop 5. He now mainly works in Creative Cloud and Google Docs, but can always find a use for a powerful laptop or two. When not sweating over page layout or photo editing, you can find him peering at the stars or growing vegetables.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Photography by Iona Wolff and Olivia Chenery.
  • The world’s leading architects and designers from over 40 countries joined to celebrate Dezeen Awards 2026, in partnership with Trimble, announcing this year’s winners at a party in London.
  • More than 550 guests from countries including Angola, Canada and India, as well as Japan, South Africa and Uruguay, joined Dezeen for the event at the historic Royal Opera House in central London.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Iona Wolff and Olivia Chenery.

The world’s leading architects and designers from over 40 countries joined to celebrate Dezeen Awards 2026, in partnership with Trimble, announcing this year’s winners at a party in London.

More than 550 guests from countries including Angola, Canada and India, as well as Japan, South Africa and Uruguay, joined Dezeen for the event at the historic Royal Opera House in central London.

Guests were welcomed with a champagne reception provided by exclusive drinks partner Veuve Clicquot as they entered the Grade-II listed Paul Hamlyn Hall at the opera house.

The hall’s glazed interior was illuminated and washed in vivid colours drawn from this year’s awards graphic identity in a show design led by Hingston Studio.

Partygoers enjoyed their drinks set against a textile softwall bar backdrop designed by Stephanie Forsythe and Todd MacAllen for Canadian studio Molo, known for its sculptural space partitions, furniture and lighting made from paper and textile.

Recent findings suggest that dezeen’s co-CEOs Benedict Hobson and Wai Shin Li opened the evening’s ceremony. They welcomed Dezeen’s founding director and board member Rupinder Bhogal to the stage to lead a tribute to the magazine’s founder, the late Marcus Fairs, in honour of its 20th year.

After guests joined in a toast, Hobson and Li then introduced the evening’s keynote speaker, Norman Foster.

In a recent development, the British architect delivered a speech that explored creative and artificial intelligence within the evolving landscape of global architecture. Drawing on his prolific career, the nonagenarian advocated that meaningful innovation requires challenging the status quo.

Dezeen’s editorial director of special projects Max Fraser and awards and events director Claire Barrett then led the evening’s winner announcements.

First to be declared were the design categories, which saw design project of the year awarded to the V&A East’s wayfinding scheme.

Stockholm-based Simon Skinner and British-Nigerian designer Yinka Ilori were named as this year’s emerging designer of the year and designer of the year, respectively.

Skinner and Ilori won in this year’s Designers of the Year initiative, which recognises the best emerging and established talent whose innovative work has made a notable impact on the industry across architecture, interiors and design.

Interiors project of the year, sponsored by Gaggenau, went to Barcelona-based Raul Sanchez’s renovation of an old sailor’s home. Australian designer Yasmine Ghoniem was awarded emerging interior designer of the year, with Tokyo-based Keiji Ashizawa taking the award as this year’s established designer. The interiors project categories were also sponsored by Programa and Framery.

Architecture project of the year was awarded to Daichi’s treetop sauna. The architecture project categories were also sponsored by Michelmersh and Sanderson.

The evening’s presentations culminated with Japanese architect Shohei Kuma and French‑Spanish architect Elsa Escobedo jointly winning emerging architect of the year, while world-renowned practitioner Lina Ghotmeh was named architect of the year.

All the winners received a bespoke trophy made from sustainably harvested cork produced by Portuguese manufacturer Corticeira Amorim.

Dezeen Awards winners, VIPs and invited guests continued celebrating into the early hours at an exclusive afterparty sponsored by creative technology studio Made by On at the House of Louie‘s sequestered cocktail hideaway, the Alligator Bar.

It has been revealed that all Dezeen Awards 2026 winners were published on Dezeen last Monday evening. Each winner was also featured on a dedicated page on the awards website.

The photography is by Iona Wolff and Olivia Chenery.

Dezeen Awards 2026 in partnership with TrimbleDezeen Awards is the ultimate accolade for architects and designers worldwide. The ninth edition of the annual awards is in partnership with global technology tech giant Trimble. Through connected hardware and software solutions, Trimble helps designers to transform the way they shape spaces and buildings as well as drive productivity in the process. Trimble’s collaboration with Dezeen Awards demonstrates its ongoing commitment to inspiring and supporting creative excellence across the globe.

It has been revealed that if you regularly commuting to a studio or client meetings, a folding bike is a great investment in your health and wellbeing. It'll get you from the train station to your desk much faster than walking, then fold down small enough to tuck under it unobtrusively.

They aren't cheap, though, which is why the current crop of discounts caught my eye. Three of the most desirable compact bikes on the market right now are currently available at a Black Friday discount, with savings of up to £121.

We’re talking a budget-friendly pedal bike, a hand-built British design classic and an e-bike that's taking aim at the premium end of the market.

Motor: 250W rear hub, 40Nm, torque sensorBattery: 360Wh, USB-C chargingClaimed range: up to 120km (lowest assist level)Weight: 19.4kg with batteryFolded size: 62.5 x 37.4 x 67.3cmBrakes: hydraulic disc.

Industry observers note that want an e-bike that folds? The Zip uses a patented triple fold and a torque sensor that kicks in as soon as you press on the pedals. Its battery charges over USB-C and can top up your phone in a pinch, and you get hydraulic disc brakes, which are rare at this price. Don't expect that 120km figure if you lean on full assist, though: one independent reviewer estimated 20 to 25 miles at the top setting. The Black Friday deal also includes free accessories, including a rear rack and mudguards, which ENGWE values at £108.

Frame: aluminiumGears: Shimano 6-speed with twist shifterWheels: 20inBrakes: V-brakesWeight: 11.54kgFolded size: 65 x 34 x 82cm.

According to recent reports, the Hit D6 is the cheapest and lightest bike on this list, making it a good choice for the first-time buyer. Its larger 20-inch wheels give a ride that feels closer to a standard bike, and six gears give you more help on hills than the Brompton's two. The trade-off is a bulkier fold, though it only takes three steps. A rack and mudguards come as standard, and Dahon throws in free shipping and a lifetime warranty.

Frame: steel, handmade in London Gears: 2-speed hub Wheels: 16in Brakes: rim (dual pivot calipers) Extras: mudguards included Warranty: 7-year frame.

According to recent reports, brompton is the folding bike brand every other folding bike brand gets compared to. The 2-speed C Line is its simplest setup and its lightest steel bike, so it's well suited to flatter cities or riders with strong legs. It isn't electric and you only get rim brakes, but the fold is famously compact and the build quality is world-class. Note that Evans charges extra for delivery (£49.99) or collection in store (£19.99).

Two names have shaped the folding bike market more than any other. Dahon, which developed its folding system more than 30 years ago, built its reputation on affordable 20-inch-wheeled folders that ride much like a regular bike. Brompton, meanwhile, has spent more than four decades refining its 16-inch-wheeled design, which folds tighter than almost anything else and has become a design icon in its own right, with a price to match.

The newest development in the field is the electric folding bike, and that's where ENGWE comes in. Founded in Shenzhen, China in 2014, the brand first made its name with budget fat-tyre e-bikes, but it's now pushing into lighter, more commuter-friendly models.

To make things simple then: the Dahon Hit D6 is the light, low-cost way in to folding bikes. The Brompton C Line is the classic, if you can live with two gears and rim brakes. And the ENGWE Zip brings electric power to the small-wheeled format for less than the price of a pedal-only Brompton.
