  • It has been revealed that five years after the Jehovah’s Witnesses sued the German government over ownership of an archive tracing one family’s persecution by the Nazi regime, the files have been returned to the religious organization, reports the Latest York Times.
  • The more than 1,000 documents, photographs, drawings, letters, and reports that make up the archive were collected and saved for decades by Annemarie Kusserow, one of 11 children from a Jehovah’s Witness family that lived in the town of Bad Lippspringe in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany.
  • At the time of her death in 2005, Annemarie Kusserow’s will stated that her family’s archive should go to the Jehovah’s Witnesses.

It has been revealed that five years after the Jehovah’s Witnesses sued the German government over ownership of an archive tracing one family’s persecution by the Nazi regime, the files have been returned to the religious organization, reports the Latest York Times. Jehovah’s Witnesses were targeted by the Nazis specifically for their refusal to salute Hitler, display the swastika flag, or serve in the military; 4,500 were sent to concentration camps, and 1,800 died during the Nazi era.

The more than 1,000 documents, photographs, drawings, letters, and reports that make up the archive were collected and saved for decades by Annemarie Kusserow, one of 11 children from a Jehovah’s Witness family that lived in the town of Bad Lippspringe in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany. According to an oral history published by the U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum, the Kusserow home was searched by the Gestapo 20 times, and the Kusserow parents, Hilda and Franz, were the first to be arrested, in the mid-1930s. The children eventually ended up in prisons, concentration camps, or training schools. Two brothers, Wilhelm and Wolfgang, were murdered by the Nazis, and another survived the war but died shortly after from tuberculosis contracted at Dachau. Related Articles Hamburg Culture Prize Renamed After Namesake's Nazi Ties Emerge Switzerland's Bührle Foundation Reaches Settlement with Heirs of Jewish Collector Who Owned Prized Manet.

At the time of her death in 2005, Annemarie Kusserow’s will stated that her family’s archive should go to the Jehovah’s Witnesses. But one of her brothers, Hans Werner Kusserow, had the archive in his possession at the time, and in 2009 he sold it to the Bundeswehr Military History Museum in Dresden. This was “especially troubling,” the Jehovah’s Witnesses’ official website notes, given that her brothers lost their lives due to their pacifism.

Industry observers note that the parties came to an “amicable agreement” on November 19, which was formalized the following day by the Higher Regional Court of Cologne. The museum and the Jehovah’s Witnesses agreed to keep the details of the settlement private. A Kusserow relative told the New York Times it is “a great relief that at last we will have these precious documents back where Annemarie always wanted them.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thelma Golden, the director and chief curator of the Studio Museum in Harlem, will step down from her position in late 2027, the museum announced Tuesday.

Recent findings suggest that the announcement coincides with Golden’s 20th anniversary in the role, which she assumed in 2006, and comes just one year after the museum reopened in a new, purpose-built building after a seven-year closure. The new $125 million building was designed by architect David Adjaye and provides 82,000 square feet across seven floors, including a 139-seat public lobby, a rooftop terrace, education spaces, a library, and a cafe. It received rave reviews upon its reopening. Related Articles Zohran Mamdani Spends a Birthday to Remember at the Studio Museum in Harlem Time Magazine Publishes its First Art 100 List, Featuring Artists, Museum Leaders, Dealers and More--See Who Made the Cut.

Kathryn C. Chenault, chair of the museum’s board of trustees, stated in a statement that the board has formed a search committee to identify Golden’s successor and has retained an international executive search firm to assist. Golden will remain in her post until a replacement is hired.

It has been revealed that while Golden’s departure was not entirely expected, it is not unusual for museum directors to exit their positions after a major renovation or expansion. Lisa Phillips revealed in September 2025 that she would leave her role as director of the Fresh Museum after its reopening, and Janne Sirén, director of the Buffalo AKG Art Museum, said in April that he would step down following the museum’s 2023 expansion.

“I know this is the right moment to begin this transition—and as I look ahead to upcoming projects and opportunities, I also look back with gratitude toward the many people whose achievements have been my bedrock,” Golden said in a statement. “I think of my teachers, mentors, and professional colleagues; the long line of Directors, Trustees, and donors who established the Studio Museum and made it thrive; half a century’s worth of endlessly dedicated staff members, audiences, and beloved Harlem neighbors; and above all the generations of artists who have enlightened us. Together, they are an expansive community I cherish that will continue to inspire and enable the next leader of the Studio Museum.”.

Before becoming director of the Studio Museum, Golden worked there as a curatorial fellow. She then joined the Whitney Museum of American Art in 1988 as a curatorial assistant and held several curatorial positions there, co-organizing the 1993 Whitney Biennial and organizing the landmark 1994 exhibition “Black Male: Representations of Masculinity in American Art.” In 2000, she returned to the Studio Museum as deputy director for exhibitions and programs under then-director Lowery Stokes Sims. When Sims stepped down in 2005, Golden was named as her successor.

Sources indicate that golden has been credited with raising the profile of the Studio Museum through numerous groundbreaking exhibitions, including 2001’s “Freestyle”. Organized with curator Christine Y. Kim, the show featured 28 emerging Black artists whose work the curators described as “post-Black.” Among the artists championed in that show were Mark Bradford, Rashid Johnson, and Julie Mehretu.

In 2023, Golden won the Dorothy and Lillian Gish Prize, which carries a $250,000 award and recognizes a person who has made a significant contribution to the arts.

Speaking to ARTnews in 2020, Golden described what the Studio Museum meant to her and other young Black creatives:.

It has been revealed that [At the Studio Museum], they begin their careers and are able to not only get real professional experience but to form a mission and get a vision of real museum work. I say this as someone whose career is the result of those early experiences at the Studio Museum. It cannot be overstated how significant it was for me, as a 19-year-old art history/African-American studies double major from Smith College, to encounter Dr. Mary Schmidt Campbell, art historian and director of the Studio Museum. I can’t tell you what it meant for me, after over a decade as a curator at the Whitney, to become chief curator at the Studio Museum and to work for Dr. Lowery Stokes Sims, a pioneer in the museum field.

Venice Biennale Awards Selected by Public Vote Go to Nick Cave, Indian Pavilion

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that after a Venice Biennale of bitter controversy, the exhibition has at last revealed the winners of its top honors, which were chosen this year by public vote instead of a jury of esteemed curators because that panel resigned in protest.
  • Dubbed the Visitors’ Lions, these awards replaced the Golden Lions, which are regularly given to participants in the main exhibition and artists representing countries with pavilions in the exhibition.
  • The Biennale was forced to instate the Visitors’ Lions after the five-person Golden Lion jury resigned in May, in advance of the show’s opening.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that after a Venice Biennale of bitter controversy, the exhibition has at last revealed the winners of its top honors, which were chosen this year by public vote instead of a jury of esteemed curators because that panel resigned in protest. This time around, the awards went to the American artist Nick Cave for his participation in Koyo Kouoh’s main exhibition and India for its national pavilion.

Dubbed the Visitors’ Lions, these awards replaced the Golden Lions, which are regularly given to participants in the main exhibition and artists representing countries with pavilions in the exhibition. This time around, just two awards were given out, one for an artist in the main show and one for a national pavilion. Related Articles In Sammy Baloji's Hands, 'Objective' Materials Reveal Latest Truths About African History Actor Says He Removed His Mother's Art from Venice Biennale Installation as a Pro-Israel Protest.

The Biennale was forced to instate the Visitors’ Lions after the five-person Golden Lion jury resigned in May, in advance of the show’s opening. By that point, the curators had already said that they would “refrain from considering those countries whose leaders are at the moment charged with crimes against humanity by the International Criminal Court,” a move that would exclude Israel and Russia from consideration. More than half of the artists in the main show said they would not accept the Visitors’ Lions in solidarity.

Cave’s contributions to the Kouoh’s show, titled “In Minor Keys,” included a decidedly major work: Amalgam (Origin), a 26-foot-tall bronze sculpture in which a person’s body sprouts branches and wildlife. The work, which appeared outdoors at the Arsenale, derived from a similar-looking proposal for a piece to replace a toppled Confederate monument.

It has been revealed that inside and outside the Arsenale, there were yet more large-scale Cave sculptures that composed Two Points in Time – At Once, which featured more figures whose bodies fuse with plants. Needlepointed portraits accompanied those figures. “The works address the stages of grief toward mourning, rebirth, and radical connection,” Cave wrote on social media in May, when the Biennale opened.

India’s pavilion, titled “Geographies of Distance: Remembering Home,” dealt largely with how objects act as vessels for memories and featured such grandly sized pieces as Sumakshi Singh’s Permanent Address, in which the walls of a house were remade in see-through thread, causing the domicile to appear flimsy and impermanent.

According to recent reports, alongside Singh, the pavilion featured works by Alwar Balasubramaniam, Ranjani Shettar, Asim Waqif, and Skarma Sonam Tashi. Organized by curator Amin Jaffer, the pavilion was the first staged by India at the Biennale since 2019.

In a statement posted to social media, the Indian ministry of culture mentioned, “The recognition highlights the talent of Indian artists and the growing global presence of contemporary Indian art.”.

The Biennale’s spare release unusually did not include citations for why the Indian Pavilion and Cave won, likely because neither had been selected by a jury. Instead, the release included a statement from Biennale president Pietrangelo Buttafuoco, who remarked, “The public of the Exhibition embraced this recognition – the Visitors’ Award – as an opportunity to bring Pablo Picasso’s practice to life: a painting only comes to life through the person who looks at it. I can say without hesitation that La Biennale is brimming with ever-renewed energy thanks to the vibrant presence of everyone.”.

When the Biennale opened, dozens of participants in Kouoh’s main exhibition, as well as several dozen more with national pavilions, signed a statement saying that they did not want to be considered for the Visitors’ Lions as a form of solidarity with the resigned jury. If these artists were selected as winners, they said, the Biennale could expect legal action. “Not only is this confusing for visitors, it is blatantly disrespectful towards the artists who have made the request for removal of their names,” the artists said in a statement.

Though it did not directly respond to the artists, the Biennale said in its release about the Visitors’ Lions that “all national participations” were eligible, since the exhibition is about “openness, dialogue, and the rejection of any form of closure or censorship.”.

Notably, neither Cave nor the artists representing India signed the e-flux statement, which was endorsed by many of the artists with most talked-about pavilions in Venice—including Florentina Holzinger, whose Austrian Pavilion generated long lines and emerged as an early favorite during the professional preview.

In a recent development, the Visitors’ Lions bring to an end a tumultuous Biennale marked by protests over Israel and Russia’s pavilions, which faced an outcry both before and during the Biennale, with many calling for both countries to be ejected altogether. The Biennale sought to proclaim itself a neutral entity, saying that it cannot kick out any nation recognized as a state by the Italian government. But the logic proved unpersuasive for many, including the European Union, which mentioned it will revoke a 2 million euro grant that it typically awards to the Biennale as a protest against the Russian Pavilion’s return this year, during a period when Russia continues to face EU sanctions over its war in Ukraine.

Lifetime achievement prizes are typically revealed ahead of the Biennale’s opening, but none were awarded this time because Kouoh, the curator of the main show, died in 2025 before she could select the winners. A Silver Lion, for a promising young artist in the main exhibition, was not awarded during this round, either, likely because that prize is given out by a jury who was not present to offer it.

The Biennale has positioned this year’s fraught edition as a resounding success. Upon its closure this past weekend, the Biennale said the show received more than 714,000 visitors, the second-highest attendance figure in the exhibition’s history. “This edition of the Biennale, so rich in events and complex developments—so immersed in the harsh affairs of the world—was pervaded by a vivid spirit, rewarded indeed by the number of visitors,” Buttafuoco, the Biennale president, said in a statement this past weekend.

According to recent reports, the Biennale was initially expected to announce the Visitors’ Lions when the exhibition concluded its run on Sunday. Asked by ARTnews about the delay, a Biennale spokesperson stated that extra time was necessary to “ensure that sufficient time is available to complete the necessary overall vote count.”.

#126755. Preserving Henry Ford’s failed Amazonian empire

Preserving Henry Ford’s failed Amazonian empire

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1210 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Deep in the Amazon Rainforest, in the Brazilian state of Pará, lies the dilapidated settlement of Fordlândia.
  • In a recent development, earlier this year, almost a century after Fordlândia was built, a federal court ruled that it must be protected as a heritage site under the Brazilian constitution.
  • Ford’s firm originally acquired the land for what would become Fordlândia in 1927.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Deep in the Amazon Rainforest, in the Brazilian state of Pará, lies the dilapidated settlement of Fordlândia. A once bustling—albeit highly exploitative—village, it was established by the US industrialist Henry Ford in the 1920s. Fordlândia’s sole purpose was to serve as a rubber-tapping enterprise that would provide materials for the Ford Motor Organization. But less than a decade after its founding, the rubber crops failed. With the development of synthetic rubber following close behind, Ford abandoned the project in 1945, and the village along the Tapajós River fell into severe disrepair.

In a recent development, earlier this year, almost a century after Fordlândia was built, a federal court ruled that it must be protected as a heritage site under the Brazilian constitution. Local and national authorities have until the end of this month to come up with a conservation blueprint.

Ford’s firm originally acquired the land for what would become Fordlândia in 1927. He envisioned building a Midwestern-style village as a hub for latex extraction, supplying materials for his factories in Michigan. Ford hoped to upend the dominance of British-controlled rubber plantations in Southeast Asia, which had left US manufacturers dependent on foreign suppliers.

Fordlândia, beyond giving the Ford Motor Tech giant control over its supply of raw materials, was imagined as a self-sufficient settlement for around 10,000 people in the Amazon. Ford himself viewed Fordlândia as a sociological experiment intended to “Americanise” the local population, although the tycoon never visited his dystopian village. Workers there, many of them Indigenous people and migrants from northeastern Brazil, endured cultural subjugation and often faced dangerous conditions—including having to work through the hottest part of the day. Hundreds of people died during the short-lived project.

Sources indicate that workers organised a mutiny in 1930 after unreasonable restrictions were imposed in Fordlândia, including the prohibition of alcohol and tobacco, as well as the requirement of US customs like square dancing and a diet of wholewheat bread, brown rice, oatmeal and canned peaches. Shortly afterwards there was a full-scale riot, in which workers chased their American managers and the village cook into the jungle. The Brazilian army was brought in to restore order. The firm subsequently fired a number of workers and appointed a newly introduced manager to complete Fordlândia’s infrastructure. (An agreement on serving different food to the workers was also reached.).

Fordlândia Dance Hall, around 1933 The Collections of the Henry Ford.

Ford’s social experiment unfolded alongside agricultural problems. Without the consultation of local experts, the rubber trees had been planted too close together. This made them vulnerable to disease and pests, and the growing conditions along the river were unsuitable. In 1933, at the recommendation of the American plant pathologist James Robert Weir, a second plantation was established downstream at Belterra, where conditions were more appropriate. Although it fared better than Fordlândia, production remained costly and it never became commercially viable.

It has been revealed that no usable latex was ever produced in Fordlândia. After investing millions of dollars with no return, Ford sold the land back to the Brazilian government. The population dropped by more than 90% in the following years, but squatters and families moved back into the decaying structures in the 2000s. Around 3,000 people live in Fordlândia today, even as the village remains unconnected to paved roads.

The federal process for the designation of Fordlândia as a heritage site has been unresolved since the 1990s, when the move was first suggested by local advocates. In 2015, Brazil’s federal public prosecutor’s office filed a lawsuit stating that the site had “unquestionable” cultural value. In 2024, the National Institute of Historic and Artistic Heritage (Iphan) countered that Fordlândia lacked the criteria required for federal heritage listing, pointing to the loss of its original characteristics and the site’s deteriorated condition.

Sources indicate that but in May 2026 a federal court ruled that, even without formal heritage status, the site should be protected. This decision was based on a 1988 constitutional article that mandates the conservation of both material and immaterial assets connected to Brazilian communities. The court added that uncertainty over ownership of the site had been used repeatedly as justification for inaction, and that the state of Pará and the municipality of Aveiro (which administers Fordlândia) had previously signed an agreement to begin conservation measures that never materialised. It also alleged that some interventions had been carried out without authorisation.

A Fordlândia sawmill in 1931, before the Ford Motor Tech giant’s rubber-plantation project was halted The Collections of the Henry Ford.

The court ruled that Iphan must now work with the state and municipality to deliver a initiative by the end of November 2026, outlining the responsibilities of each government entity and the needs of each site in Fordlândia—including emergency measures for structures at imminent risk. Once approved, conservation work must begin within 30 days. If deadlines are not met, the court will impose a daily fine of $2,000 (10,000 reais) on the federal government and Iphan, and a $1,000 (5,000 reais) fine on the state and municipality. Iphan must also begin the administrative process to recognise Fordlândia as a heritage site.

In a statement to The Art Newspaper, a spokesperson for Iphan says the agency does not comment on ongoing legal proceedings. It remains unclear if Iphan prepares to counter the court’s decision. “In May 2024, Iphan’s cultural-heritage advisory council denied Fordlândia’s designation as Brazilian cultural heritage,” the spokesperson says. “Iphan reiterates that it remains committed to the preservation of Brazilian cultural heritage, as mandated by the constitution.”.

The sites to be reviewed include the former Fordlândia Hospital, designed by the Detroit architect Albert Kahn; the long-abandoned industrial and port warehouses; the houses of the American Village, where the organization’s American managers lived; the workers’ village; the Henry Ford School; the Cine Patinha, a cinema whose roof has recently collapsed; and a convent on a cliff overlooking the Tapajós River, built in the post-Ford era and active until the early 2010s. All these structures have been exposed to the Amazon’s heat, humidity and heavy rainfall for years.

It has been revealed that fordlândia remains highly remote, receiving few outside visitors and requiring a minimum six-hour trip to reach via high-speed boat. Still, there is evidence that intrepid travellers have made the journey. A manufacturer specialising in tours of the Amazon is presently offering a five-day visit to the region, including a stop in Fordlândia, for approximately $3,000 (16,000 reais) per person. Reviews for “Fordlândia Ghost Town” on TripAdvisor average 4.7 out of 5 stars, with one reviewer in 2016 calling the site “historical, magical and melancholic”, and another saying it tells a story of “hubris, determination, paternalism and ultimately failure”.

Recent findings suggest that although Fordlândia is unlikely to be commercialised as a tourist destination, the village’s surviving infrastructure has come to represent an unusual and failed attempt to Americanise and industrialise the Amazon. The remnants of the settlement also tell the story of the Brazilian workers who lived there, and those who have continued to inhabit it. The Brazilian government maintains that Fordlândia has “unquestionable historical, cultural and architectural value”, and that it represents “an American attempt to break the British monopoly on rubber and bring modern infrastructure to the middle of the Amazon”.

One memory in particular still stings: In 2006, when Takashi Murakami left Boesky for Gagosian, she recalls that after her daughter Ellie was born, he told her he couldn’t be represented by someone who was “lactating.” “It was devastating for me because it was still so early in my career,” she noted. “He didn’t honor his commitments that we had made to each other. That’s when it went south.” Murakami’s studio said the artist had no recollection of saying the comment about breastfeeding. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Michael Bouhanna, the former vice president of contemporary art specialist and head of digital art at Sotheby’s, has launched his own art advisory.
  • Bouhanna was the last man standing at Sotheby’s Metaverse and other NFT divisions when the auction house laid off four staffers in 2024.
  • Bouhanna’s fresh chapter in Miami will involve placing modern and contemporary art by blue-chip artists in private collections and hands.

Michael Bouhanna, the former vice president of contemporary art specialist and head of digital art at Sotheby’s, has launched his own art advisory. Called Bouhanna Art Advisory, it will focus on modern and contemporary art based out of Miami.

Bouhanna was the last man standing at Sotheby’s Metaverse and other NFT divisions when the auction house laid off four staffers in 2024. He joined the company in 2016 as CTP junior cataloger and promptly moved up the ranks in the contemporary art department before being given the joint responsibility of contemporary and digital art in 2021. Bouhanna exited Sotheby’s in January, after just over a decade at the auction house working in its London, Paris, and Fresh York headquarters. Bouhanna’s exit was unrelated to the layoffs, although following his departure Sotheby’s integrated NFTs and digital art into its contemporary art department. In September 2025, Christie’s closed its digital art department as the demand for digital art cooled down. In a wider view of the digital art market, Bouhanna told ARTnews that digital art is still part of contemporary art and it should not be seen as a separate entity. “Digital art still interests collectors who follow technology and AI. The serious digital artists have continued to gain institutional recognition, but it’s a niche within contemporary art.” Related Articles Yoshitomo Nara Painting Fetches $15.9 M., Outselling Koons and Richter in New York Led by Record-Breaking $190.4 M. van Gogh, Sotheby's Impressionist and Modern Art Sales Rake in $777.8 M.

Bouhanna’s fresh chapter in Miami will involve placing modern and contemporary art by blue-chip artists in private collections and hands. In Miami, he has started working with private collectors, family offices and estates across acquisitions, sales, valuation and the management of collections. “Miami and South Florida collectors have built serious collections over the last decade, and a new generation is entering the market at a high level and often, they’re making their first significant acquisition,” Bouhanna said. “The established and emerging collectors need sophisticated advisory services that have long been available in London, New York or Paris, and also because transactions have become more complex with guarantees, private sales, and financing, collectors need experts on their side to evaluate them more than ever.”.

Bouhanna moved to Miami earlier this year with his wife, Alexandra Benezra, founder of the public relations agency ASB PR Agency and fashion label Selvi. In the last year, he has been getting a feel for the city, which has absorbed more wealth in 10 years than any other American city and single-family offices are expected to grow by more than 10,000 by 2030. “Founders of companies, financial firms and families from the Northeast, West Coast and Latin America, who have had a strong habit of collecting art now live in South Florida,” Bouhanna said, noting that there’s also an influx of young, self-made entrepreneurs and financiers who are taking up art collection as an investment. Miami’s cultural infrastructure is following the same curve with institutions such as Pérez Art Museum Miami, ICA Miami, Bass Museum of Art and Rubell Museum offering competitive programs all year round as opposed to just one week during Art Basel Miami.

Christie’s Adds UK Auction House Dreweatts to Its Portfolio

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Christie’s has added the UK auction house Dreweatts to its portfolio.
  • Recent findings suggest that in a statement on Wednesday, Christie’s chief executive Bonnie Brennan said that the auction house has long admired Dreweatts.
  • Dreweatts specializes in single-owner collections and country house sales, ranging from furniture and works of art, old masters, modern and contemporary art, Asian and European ceramics, modern design, jewelry, silver, luxury accessories, clocks and wine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Christie’s has added the UK auction house Dreweatts to its portfolio.

Recent findings suggest that in a statement on Wednesday, Christie’s chief executive Bonnie Brennan said that the auction house has long admired Dreweatts. “Most importantly, our clients collect across categories and at every price point, and together we have the opportunity to provide them with an even broader and more complete level of service. Both businesses will continue to operate much as they do today, while building on their respective strengths and the significant opportunities we see for future growth,” she said. Related Articles Working Mothers Face Pervasive Discrimination in London Art World, Study Finds Yoshitomo Nara Painting Fetches $15.9 M., Outselling Koons and Richter in New York.

Dreweatts specializes in single-owner collections and country house sales, ranging from furniture and works of art, old masters, modern and contemporary art, Asian and European ceramics, modern design, jewelry, silver, luxury accessories, clocks and wine. The auction house was founded in 1759 by Thomas Davis, a cabinetmaker, upholsterer and land agent from Abingdon, Oxfordshire. Dreweatts operates its main salesroom from its country house, Donnington Priory, in Newbury, Berkshire, and also has a showroom in London on Pall Mall.

Henry House, chief executive of Dreweatts, said in a statement that under this new arrangement “we can use the additional advantage of one another’s expertise to better serve our buyers and sellers. Dreweatts has had a parent tech giant before, which enabled us to grow the business and prosper, and this move is an extension of that model.” He added that the Christie’s acquisition provides certainty for the auction house and that Dreweatts will continue, under his and chairman Will Richards’ stewardship.

Christie’s president of EMEA, Anthea Peers, said that the François Pinault-owned auction house recognized Dreweatts as a “healthy, compatible business to our own and the value it can add to what we do for all of our clients.”.

According to recent reports, on November 19, Dreweatts presented its Fine Watches & Luxury Accessories auction that totaled £529,934 with an 89% sell-through rate. The sale included fine watches, designer handbags, writing instruments and luxury objects from Patek Philippe, Cartier, Hermès, Chanel and Montblanc. The top lots were a Lange & Söhne that sold for £49,780 and a Montblanc black porcelain fountain pen that sold for £8,320.

The Witcher 4 is aiming for a GTA 6-sized leap in graphics

💡 Key Takeaways
  • GTA 6 is having a wider impact than just being one of the highest-rated games ever, with a 99 on Metacritic; it’s making other developers rethink what they’re doing.
  • In a recent development, the impact of GTA 6 is simple: it’s as impressive as all great art is, because it expands what's possible through a captivating vision and flawless execution.
  • CD Projekt Red is no slouch when it comes to technically advanced games and graphics, but even they are having that moment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GTA 6 is having a wider impact than just being one of the highest-rated games ever, with a 99 on Metacritic; it’s making other developers rethink what they’re doing. This week, many devs came out and praised GTA 6’s technical achievements, from CD Projekt Red to Naughty Dog, but behind the scenes, those same creators are setting new benchmarks to complete.

In a recent development, the impact of GTA 6 is simple: it’s as impressive as all great art is, because it expands what's possible through a captivating vision and flawless execution. And it’s making developers think and rethink.

CD Projekt Red is no slouch when it comes to technically advanced games and graphics, but even they are having that moment. The studio behind The Witcher 3 and Cyberpunk 2077 has admitted that GTA 6 inspires its developers, with joint CEO Michał Nowakowski saying he expects The Witcher 4 to make a similarly huge leap over its predecessor.

Recent findings suggest that as reported on Polygon, speaking during the company's latest investor call, Nowakowski was asked whether the jump from The Witcher 3 to The Witcher 4 would be comparable to the one between GTA 5 and GTA 6. His answer was pretty emphatic.

"Do we believe there's going to be a comparable leap between Witcher 3 and Witcher 4? I think so, yes," he said. "I mean, it's been 11 years.".

The studio is working to make The Witcher 4 "significantly better-looking and improved in terms of pretty much every possible facet of the game", adding that players should expect a much bigger jump between the two games.

According to recent reports, that's quite a promise, although there's a good reason to be ambitious. The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt is now 11 years old, and while its world still looks fantastic (especially after its recent remaster), the technology and expectations for open-world games have moved on considerably.

Industry observers note that GTA 6 is an obvious comparison, but I'm more interested in what CD Projekt Red does differently. Rockstar has its own way of building a world, and The Witcher's appeal has always been its atmosphere, character design, and strong writing. I don't need Ciri's world to look like Vice City, but I do want the same depth and sense of a living world Rockstar has created. Following this year’s Unreal Engine 5.6 tech demo, I’m sure The Witcher 4 will impress, possibly setting a new standard.

CD Projekt Red is clearly putting a lot of its development resources into The Witcher 4. Its latest figures show 513 developers working on the game, compared with 199 on Cyberpunk 2. The latter is still in the earlier stages of development, so expect that team to grow. The Witcher 4 is presently targeting a 2028 release, while Cyberpunk 2 is further away, and by that time we’ll be in the realms of PlayStation 6 and Unreal Engine 6.

There's also a question of how much money studios need to spend to reach these new visual standards. Nowakowski was keen to stress that GTA 6 hasn't changed CD Projekt Red's development philosophy, describing its projects as ambition-driven rather than simply budget-driven.

Perhaps that's where the GTA 6 hype is sidelined: few developers have Rockstar’s billion-dollar budgets, and no indie ever will, but CD Projekt Red has UE6 and faith in its artists, technicians, and writers. You still need artists with a clear idea of what they want to create, and developers who know how to bring that vision to life.

#126748. Five Questions for Advisors on the November Marquee Sales: Guarantees, Spotty Bidding, and a $190 M. Van Gogh

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3517 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Artnews ↗ Open Full Page

Five Questions for Advisors on the November Marquee Sales: Guarantees, Spotty Bidding, and a $190 M. Van Gogh

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3517 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Artnews

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s Thanksgiving week and, for those of us who live and breathe the art market, that means only the briefest of breaks between the all-vital November auction season and the year’s grand finale at Art Basel Miami Beach.
  • Perhaps more than in any other industry, the health of the art market is in the eye of the beholder.
  • Industry observers note that according to data from ARTDAI, the November evening sales at Christie’s, Sotheby’s, and Phillips generated $2.03 billion, a modest 7.5 percent increase over 2025, but the highest total since 2022.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s Thanksgiving week and, for those of us who live and breathe the art market, that means only the briefest of breaks between the all-vital November auction season and the year’s grand finale at Art Basel Miami Beach. But before we turn to Miami, a quick post-mortem on the marquee sales just passed.

Perhaps more than in any other industry, the health of the art market is in the eye of the beholder. Do you measure it by overall totals? By sell-through rate? By the number of bidders, or the number of guaranteed lots? By the ratio of hammer prices to estimates? Each figure tells a slightly different story, leaving plenty for our resident market whisperers to debate. But before we turn this week’s column over to the advisers, let’s set out some basic figures.

Industry observers note that according to data from ARTDAI, the November evening sales at Christie’s, Sotheby’s, and Phillips generated $2.03 billion, a modest 7.5 percent increase over 2025, but the highest total since 2022. Sotheby’s led the pack with $1.16 billion, clearing $1 billion and taking more than half of the three houses’ combined total for the second straight year. (Its share rose to 57 percent from 53 percent. Christie’s share dropped to 38 percent from 43 percent, while Phillips’s ticked up to 5 percent from 4 percent, pushed by the $44.6 million Modigliani sculpture.).

According to recent reports, and yes, the $384 million gap between Sotheby’s and Christie’s is roughly what the Blaquier-Arrieta collection brought in on its own: $412 million on just 12 lots. Winning those big consignments really does matter.

Sources indicate that but for all those gaudy totals, there was a definite sense watching the week’s sales that bidding was uneven, thin, and at times absent entirely. Blame fickle collectors, sure, but it seems the auction houses pushed their estimates to the limit. Per ARTDAI, hammer prices across the various-owner sales in November 2025 came in 17 percent above the low estimates and at roughly 80 percent of the high estimates. This season, hammer prices for the same sales (i.e. excluding the Blaquier-Arrieta single-owner sale) were flat against the low estimates and just 69 percent of the highs. As Sotheby’s CEO Charles Stewart noted after the Blaquier-Arrieta sale last week, “Our estimates weren’t shy.”.

In a recent development, but does an aggressive auction house make for a weak market? Or is this the same market we’ve seen for the last few cycles—one that is choosy, blue-chip and provenance-driven, and competitive for the right objects—just approached differently by the specialists? That’s what we asked the advisers, along with their takes on everything from the spread of guarantees to that $190 million van Gogh.

Answers have been edited for clarity and concision.

According to recent reports, evan Beard, Beard & Co: Our having to repeatedly chase Impressionist and Modern Day Sale works well above the high estimates with a fairly low hit rate tells us that the “flight to safety” is more than just a tired cliché. Even second- and third-tier Impressionists performed very well.

According to recent reports, liz Sterling, Sterling | Teel Capital: The strong result for the Jeff Koons Bob-Tail [at Sotheby’s] was a pleasant reminder that no matter how highly orchestrated evening sales have become, there are still surprises. Equally, the results for the small Robert Ryman and Robert Rauschenberg from the Agnes Gund collection clearly demonstrate that there is still connoisseurship in the market.

Recent findings suggest that nina del Rio, del Rio | Byers: I have always believed the market is driven by the number of participants; more bidders = higher prices, more volatility, and less predictability. The current moment feels more predictable, safe, and tempered—which would signal fewer bidders. Estimates were full, reflecting strong performance over the past few seasons, and the buyers are still there for the majority of material, which is European Impressionism and modernism and American postwar abstraction, but there was less competition and flatter prices as a result.

Sources indicate that however, I was surprised by the sober bidding on the truly rare material, which represented a singular (once-in-a-lifetime) opportunity for buyers. Monday evening after the Sotheby’s The Now and Contemporary auction, I told ARTnews I was excited for the Blaquier sale on Wednesday because of the rarity and quality of the works; well, I was wrong that rarity would translate into bidder competition and runaway prices. The fact is, each work was priced at the top end of the artists’ (very mature) markets—leaving little room for price discovery, and bidding was thin and tempered as a result. Did buyers perceive these prices as the very top end of the market? Yes, I think so, which meant little to no competition for great works.

Maria Brito: Believe it or not, the moment that caught my attention happened in Stockholm, with the sale of Hilma af Klint’s Ser III No. 5. It hammered at 108 million Swedish kronor against a high estimate of 8 million, an extraordinary 13.5 times the estimate! Here is an artist whose importance to the history of abstraction has been celebrated by major museums for years, but whose market barely existed because so few of her abstract paintings ever became available. And suddenly collectors were fighting to pay nearly $13 million for one.

Industry observers note that we saw something similar with Aaron Douglas’s Harriet Tubman in New York, which sparked a seven-minute bidding war involving eight bidders and sold for $14.48 million against a high estimate of $3.5 million. I think this tells us something fascinating about today’s market. There is enormous capital available for historically significant, genuinely rare works, particularly by artists whose contributions have been undervalued. Collectors are willing to reconsider established price hierarchies, and when they really want something, they’re not shy about spending.

Allan Schwartzman, Schwartzman&: For me, there were several standout points: the fever for hot young artists at auction has passed; Robert Rauschenberg remains the most crucial innovator of the last 75 years, and yet his market remains undeservedly quiet; and behind that, Gilbert & George are a crazy bargain; even though their work is photographic, they are unique and should be commanding the prices of the great painters of their generation.

According to recent reports, erica Samuels, Samuels Creative: Beyond prices, this week highlighted a distinct mood across the field. There is a strong sense of collegiality—advisors, dealers, and auction houses are actively working together to ensure success for their clients amid a generally sideways market. The market relies as much on goodwill as it does on capital, and both were evident this week. Despite broader tech and financial shifts, such as the Anthropic IPO, this remains a human-driven market centered on human-made art.

Sources indicate that danielle Forest Brandi, Beaumont Nathan: There were a few revealing moments for us, but among them was the spectacular result for Monet’s La Barque. The price of $6.9 million was, on the one hand, a surprising result for a work that measured only 2 by 3 inches, but on the other hand, a good case study for how collectors are behaving at the top end of the market. Looking at that alone, it’s perhaps an irrational result, but when you think about the rarity of the object, the story, and how good that picture will look on someone’s wall, i.e., styled alongside their Chinese porcelain collection and Nakashima furniture, it starts to make sense. That’s how collectors are thinking right now; it’s the beauty of the art market and what makes collecting different from other pursuits.

In a recent development, evan Beard: Two key themes drove the high third-party guarantee rate this season: (1) Much of the material came from single-owner sales that carried house guarantees—Blaquier, Baum, Clive Davis, etc.—so the houses had to put the risk off on third parties. (2) Consignor expectations were elevated coming off a strong spring season, which pushed estimates to a level that the houses felt more comfortable locking in guarantees rather than risk a lot going unsold.

According to recent reports, guarantees are fundamental at this point. They’re a behavior tool to get an early bid from a buyer and a behavioral tool to give comfort to a consignor. Both sides still have the chance at upside. Guarantees are an crucial lubricant.

Nina del Rio: Estimates were high across both auction houses, reflecting the past six years of consistent demand and solid performance—especially for European modernism and postwar American abstraction. The auction houses agree to full estimates to compete for consignments. My guess is that Christie’s was less willing to offer house guarantees which were not backed by irrevocable bids at the start of the consignment-getting season. And Sotheby’s had a bit more faith that they would find an IB [irrevocable bid] later in the process. In brief, I believe Sotheby’s appetite for risk—and possibly their confidence in the market—was a bit stronger this season.

Industry observers note that maria Brito: Sotheby’s just revealed its biggest-ever week of fine art sales at $1.31 billion, which is extraordinary. But let’s look underneath those numbers. Almost a third of that total came from just 12 paintings in the Blaquier-Arrieta collection, all guaranteed, and the majority hammered below their low estimates. Sotheby’s guaranteed 77 percent of its evening lots compared with 47 percent at Christie’s, suggesting a much more aggressive approach to securing major consignments. Guarantees are essential to attracting exceptional property, and third-party guarantors can absorb much of the risk. But a guaranteed sale tells us little about competitive demand. What interests me is how many collectors were willing to bid beyond the guaranteed price. The money is clearly there. The willingness to compete at any price is another matter.

Allan Schwartzman: The numbers speak for themselves; I don’t have any great insights here.

It has been revealed that erica Samuels: Each house has a different appetite for risk and adapts its strategy based on the specific estate or group of works. So I think comparing things side by side is tricky because it’s not apples to apples. While guaranteeing lots significantly affects outcome variations, there is clear demand right now for artists like Warhol (Flowers, Soup Can), Celmins, and Albers in postwar, as well as Tanguy, Kandinsky, and Monet in the modern.

Recent findings suggest that danielle Forest Brandi: The IB market is relatively saturated at the moment, and there is a lot of competition. To be in the game, you need to be quick, decisive, and on the inside track. Collectors are clearly enjoying the ability to gain a competitive advantage through the IB mechanism, and it shapes behavior enormously. We find that collectors who don’t get the IB early on may not bid without it. That remarked, this season highlighted us that when the guarantees are set too high, it can take the energy out of the room and make it harder for works to inspire competitive bidding.

Evan Beard: Elevated estimates repel potential bids. Blaquier estimates crowded out potential bids. Most works get auctioned three times in a season: the auction between the houses for the material; the auction among potential guarantors; and, finally, the auction among the general public. The first two auctions erode the margin for the houses. Keeping estimates low while winning consignments is always a tricky dance.

It has been revealed that liz Sterling: I think a lot of works found their market this season regardless of where the presale estimate was set. Where presale estimates were overly aggressive, the auction houses worked hard to match reserves to bids and get works sold. Conversely, works that were conservatively estimated, such as the Aaron Douglas and Edward Hopper at Sotheby’s, saw competition and achieved prices well in excess of their presale estimates.

Nina del Rio: The markets for the high-profile works this season, which were largely European Impressionist and modern, and American Abstract Expressionist, are all relatively mature, and the top end of the artists’ prices have largely been realized. Couple this with full estimates (which the auction houses had to offer sellers to win the business) and it leaves little room for price discovery, even for the exceedingly rare Blaquier van Gogh. I believe this affected competition for the van Gogh, the entire Blaquier sale, and several other highlights across all the auction houses. However, I can’t help but wonder whether the last-minute claim on the van Gogh took other bidders out of the mix? Just a thought … and certainly not unique to me.

In a recent development, maria Brito: I think we’re reading too much into the number of bidders. In 2022, when the global art market reached its second-highest level in history, Orchard with Cypresses from the Paul Allen collection sold for $117.2 million with exactly three bidders. This week’s van Gogh also attracted three bidders, but fetched $190.4 million, more than 60 percent above the previous record. I consider Châtaigniers en fleurs a substantially better painting. Yes, it hammered at $165 million, below Sotheby’s $180 million expectation, but that doesn’t make the result disappointing. We also cannot ignore the Nazi-era provenance controversy, settled barely a day before the auction. Whether it deterred potential bidders is impossible to know. At this level of the market, buyers have extraordinary financial resources, but they still have their own ideas about value.

Sources indicate that allan Schwartzman: It brought a huge price. There were few bids because the auction houses sometimes have to stretch to get headline material. Many works that are competitively offered sell on few bids because the auction houses have already conducted an auction between themselves to get those works. This does not necessarily reflect a thin market.

Erica Samuels: I enjoy the philosophical roundabout of auction house estimates. There are different categories: the attractive, come-hither estimate; the punchy estimate; the estimate right in line with the market. It’s pretty nuanced, and you have to be careful about reading too much into them. An estimate is not a price tag. It’s a range, a suggestion. And to a certain extent, there’s a part of the auction world you only understand if you’re out there seeing a lot of things. Some artworks couldn’t sell privately, so they come to auction to try a broader audience. They may not find a buyer at any estimate.

In a recent development, but let’s be honest, it’s quite thin at the top. $190 million is a lot of money for any buyer to spend. No wonder it sold to a very seasoned professional.

Danielle Forest Brandi: The discrepancy between headline prices and estimates was a defining feature of the week. In recent years, the houses drove down estimates in an effort to revive competition, but it seems that pricing has crept back up. The thinness we saw with bidding was more indicative of these ambitious estimates than the market overall.

Evan Beard: From 2020 to 2023, we were in a pretty intense risk-on speculation cycle where emerging contemporary was hot, so a lot of that material got flipped to auction. We’re in a risk-off cycle now. So very few emerging contemporary lots need to go to auction because they are easily accessible privately. The pendulum will swing back, albeit for a upcoming group of hot young artists.

Nina del Rio: There was a lot of American postwar and contemporary material on the market last week, but few really great, major examples in the auctions. Rothko, de Kooning, Richter, Frankenthaler, and Stella (among others) were well represented with fully priced seven- and eight-figure examples, but nothing outstanding or market-making vs. the great European material on offer. (It is worth noting that women artists from the same postwar period performed better, but were still uneven—Kusama and Agnes Martin in particular.).

Industry observers note that de Kooning and Rothko are interesting case studies. While de Kooning was well represented, especially by the 1975 oil from the Hedreen collection at Sotheby’s and the Whitney’s de Kooning at Christie’s, both were fully estimated, and neither had the potential to push the artist’s market. Four Rothko paintings on paper were offered last week; one very good example sold well above estimate, and the other three examples, which were arguably not as strong, sold below estimate or were unsold.

Maria Brito: The contemporary market is suffering from serious fatigue. There are simply too many artists, too much work being produced, and too much material circulating. Collectors have become desensitized and increasingly skeptical, particularly after watching so many artists’ prices rise dramatically and then collapse.

Compare that with Impressionism and modern art, where the universe of historically established artists is considerably smaller and the supply of important works is finite. There’s a level of scarcity and historical validation that gives buyers confidence. Contemporary art is a much more crowded field, and there’s simply not enough demand to support everyone at the prices we’ve become accustomed to seeing.

Recent findings suggest that of course, exceptional artists and exceptional works will continue to command extraordinary prices, but collectors are increasingly questioning what’s genuinely worth pursuing. And I think that’s healthy.

Allan Schwartzman: The fever for hot young artists at auction is over for now. This is for several reasons: prices for most young artists for whom there was hysterical (read: speculative) buying at auction could not and did not live up to such lofty numbers; a fresh generation of artists has not emerged for which the market has the same speculative appetite (and that’s a good thing); and sometimes the market for young artists is very different at auction than at the galleries that represent artists and develop those markets.

According to recent reports, erica Samuels: Collectors are looking for historical depth far more than in previous seasons. A new wave of younger collectors is definitely entering the market. They are educated, critical thinkers who ask great questions, which makes for an exciting path forward. They want collections that move across generations of artists, not just one moment.

Sources indicate that danielle Forest Brandi: With some exceptions, the contemporary offering across both houses this season felt a bit tired in [the] view [of myself and my colleagues at Beaumont Nathan], especially in comparison to the Impressionist and modern. The depth and cultural authority of blue-chip modernism seems to offer an assuring sense of solidity and substance that is perhaps universally needed right now. Of course, tastes change, the market moves on, and in time the contemporary world will come back as that market continues to recalibrate. But in the meantime, it seems to us that collectors are more interested in the past than the present.

Evan Beard: Anyone who tells you that Gen Z is driving the art market in any meaningful way is either misinformed or trying to sell you a dream. The market is driven by a group of private equity, hedge fund, real estate, and tech entrepreneurs in their 50s and 60s. It’s the usual suspects. And each new year a few new massive buyers enter the fray. New wealth grows up and ultimately buys art. But young collectors are not a major driver at auction at the moment. How many Gen Z collectors are on the ARTnews Top 200 collectors list? Or the Forbes 400 list? Or any list? Their day is coming, though. We’ve got some young risers we’re working with.

Nina del Rio: I would be guessing if I had an answer to this question. Here’s what I know: buyer access to great quality primary market material, while still difficult and often reserved for museums, is less difficult than in the past. I believe the younger collectors are buying great material from galleries (as they should). There is less great material by living artists at auction, and the speculation in that auction market has quieted considerably.

It has been revealed that maria Brito: I didn’t see clear evidence of a major generational shift this week, but the reality is that we rarely know who the ultimate buyers are. So much of the bidding happens through advisors, dealers, and telephone representatives. The auction houses know who’s behind those paddles. The rest of us are largely guessing. There’s certainly growing participation from younger collectors, but we should distinguish between buying a $20,000 print and bidding $100 million on a painting. Younger wealth is entering the market, but I haven’t seen compelling evidence from this week’s sales that it has fundamentally changed who’s buying at the very top.

Allan Schwartzman: I was not in the room to observe live bidding.

Recent findings suggest that danielle Forest Brandi: Impressionism was clearly the dominant category during the November sales, across different levels of the market. We are seeing a growing generation of collectors who are engaged with this area and other historical categories, seeking established blue-chip names or, the inverse, overlooked artists in history like the female Surrealists. Prices across many historical areas of the market have come down from where they once were, making accessible entry points for newer collectors who want to buy things that have substance and will hold up over time.

#126746. What Is Internet Cinema?

What Is Internet Cinema?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1925 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Artnews

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Editor’s note: This story is an edition of Link Rot, a column by Shanti Escalante-De Mattei that explores the intersections of art, technology, and the internet.
  • According to recent reports, during last June’s heat wave, I found myself standing outside an unassuming office building in Crown Heights, Brooklyn, baking in the sun’s glare.
  • Once inside, I wandered around the cool, unlit space, laughing at funny paintings and sculptures until it was time to find a spot on the floor for the screening.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Editor’s note: This story is an edition of Link Rot, a column by Shanti Escalante-De Mattei that explores the intersections of art, technology, and the internet.

According to recent reports, during last June’s heat wave, I found myself standing outside an unassuming office building in Crown Heights, Brooklyn, baking in the sun’s glare. The Gallery, a nomadic curatorial platform, had set up an exhibition, titled “WeWork (oralmoral)”, in one of the building’s vacant office spaces. In celebration of the show’s closing the curators were screening films, some of which fall into the category of what is being called “internet cinema,” a burgeoning movement, or method, that has been in the making since late 2020. Related Articles Using the Graphics of GTA, Sara Sadik Explores the Challenges France's Muslim Youth Face 'Desiring Machines' Dares Us to Imagine a Healthy Relationship with Technology.

Once inside, I wandered around the cool, unlit space, laughing at funny paintings and sculptures until it was time to find a spot on the floor for the screening. Someone in front of me was hastily scrawling the lineup of the screenings on paper with a black marker and passing them around as fast as he produced them. One passed back to me. The first film on the list was Zarina Nares’ I am going to die (this is my sign) (2025). The projector was fiddled with and a rectangle of white with a buffer symbol appeared on the blank wall in front of the seated crowd.

A chorus of female voices rose up, all in some general distress, and while I couldn’t see these women, by the tone, I could tell they were speaking into a front-facing camera. The chorus cut out to a single voice, which spoke over dashcam footage of a car crash: “You’re having problems at work, your boyfriend broke up with you, your parents are mad at you, everything is going wrong, your car broke down – that is a good sign. Like, that is the very best sign.”What followed was a montage of TikTok videos featuring motivational advice. One video bled into another, linked by the formulaic hooks used by podcast bros, emotional car seat influencers, clips of celebrities’ acceptance speeches, athletes in interviews, or passionate pastors, all of which was set to music. One after another these TikToks reveal ‘the one thing that you need to learn’ in a high-speed carousel of intense emotion that feels increasingly forced as it becomes clear how many of these impassioned speeches are copies of one another.

“Internet cinema isn’t necessarily about the internet or its aesthetic but about its logic, how it functions and how it makes us feel,” Zarina Nares mentioned in a phone call. On the process of making I am going to die, she added that “Clearly, I watched enough advice videos for too long that I kept getting more. Once you watch so many you see the formula behind them, whether it’s a certain cadence of speaking or certain music.”.

Internet cinema was first defined in a 2007 paper by Chuck Tryon titled “New Media Studies and the New Internet Cinema.” The technologies and formats that concerned Tryon —iPods and camera phones, software like Final Cut Pro, and home movies—are far dated, but his paper was prescient, having tapped into impulses and concerns that reflect contemporary internet cinema: a do-it-yourself ethos that blurs the line between amateur and artist; the popularization of “niche exhibition;” and a “self-reflexive style” that works “to call attention to the narrative codes and technological specs that shape cultural productions.”.

Contemporary internet cinema has its roots in the COVID-era, which saw an explosion of participation in internet culture and production, that often bled out into one particular place: Dimes Square, a patch of Manhattan where Chinatown and the Lower East Side meet.

Industry observers note that one of the most memorable dramas that played out at the time was puppeteered by a then-anonymous internet figure who went by the name Angelicism01. This figure posted creeds about extinction on Substack, and gained infamy for growing a cult-like following among young women in Fresh York (who had never met him). With the help of various film makers, he made a three-hour long movie called Film01 which includes fast paced montages of memes, tweets, videos of natural disasters and terrorist attacks, alongside long scenes featuring the ‘it-girls’ he had recruited. Writer Madeline Cash described Film01 in the art publication Spike as “an unsophisticated collage of localized content that mimics, rather than intervenes or questions, our digital conditions,” which ultimately did nothing more than tap “into the scene’s libidinal narcissism.”Yet, with some distance, Film01 has proven to be a productive experiment. One of Angelicism01’s collaborators, the filmmaker Dana Dawud, found internet footage to splice into the film, created short edits that became a part of the larger film, and remotely directed certain sequences. Dawud would go on to launch Open Secret, an international screening series of internet cinema that has since played a large part in consolidating disconnected artists and practices under the term.At the same time that young women were running around Dimes Square at Angelicism01’s request, people were locked away at home with TikTok. More than ever, people around the world were subjecting themselves to hours and hours of scrolling on this relatively new video content platform.“When you’re doom scrolling, there is, technically speaking, no specific author to this montage that you’re watching. So, it’s as if you’re exposed to radical experimental cinema all the time by a completely cynical industrial apparatus,” noted 0nty, the co-author of “Dialogues on CoreCore & the Contemporary Online Avant-Garde” during a Zoom interview also attended by his co-author Mischa Dols. “The question is, how do you even begin to think about this problem? And I think internet cinema is an answer,” 0nty said.0nty and Dols describe internet cinema as a method, rather than a genre or an aesthetic, which seeks to expose or comment on the way that the internet functions through editing found footage.It’s worth noting that some works under the umbrella of internet cinema do feature the production of new images. Dahlia Bloomstone’s 20,000 Tokens (2025) is a screen recording of the artist chatting with men and exposing herself on the webcam site Chaturbate (the video is spliced with a glitching 3D-rendering of a blonde avatar in a black void). For The Sight is a Wound (2024), Parham Ghalamdar filmed himself burning his own paintings, as a statement on how tthe seemingly endless documentation of the genocide of Palestinians in Gaza has made images useless. Yet the particular process of editing found footage is usually highlighted in definitions of internet cinema because this method represents the folk practice that preceded internet cinema: corecore.

Core, or rather, -core, is a suffix that denotes some kind of bundle of aesthetics and moods. Cottagecore, for example, is a reference to an image universe of milkmaid tops, galoshes, a straw basket full of wildflowers, a shingled cottage, butter made with wooden tools, but also, beyond images, a wish for simple, optimistic, pastoral life. But corecore emerged not as a specific aesthetic but as a way of making video content through editing together music, clips from movies, podcasts, and other TikToks.These videos are often melancholic ruminations of the deep and unrecognized suffering of young men, the terrible sublimity of being alone with your screen, an alienated awareness of hurtling towards extinction while scrolling on your parents’ sofa. Watching compilations of corecore I reminded me intensely of my time on Tumblr as a teenager.

On Tumblr, the practice of posting and reblogging images, fragments of text, and GIFs under an “aesthetic” was a way of cultivating and nurturing a feeling: a world of images that created a visual language for all that we thought life could be. Painful, dramatic love; intensity chased by the doom of its own ephemerality; cold, beautiful suffering. In the pivot to video platforms, corecore takes that tendency to collect images and feelings and turns it into a form much more contained and shareable than a blog: the film.

Removed from the usual logics of personal branding and sponsorship deals, it became an exciting trend for those who take internet-based cultural production seriously. Corecore, as a mass movement of people making films on the same devices they watch them on, represented the realization of an old dream of experimental cinema: film as a truly collective practice.“Authorship gets really muddy, you have content creators and video artists making films on the same platforms. Dana [Dawud] has compared internet cinema to the way that SoundCloud functions, where people can steal your edit, steal your beat, steal a sample, and then it gets lost who put it online first, and that’s okay,” mentioned Edison Niebla Rodriguez, a curator who also creates video art with his wife, Dayana Matasheva, under the name Demon Lovers Inc. “Obviously, it’s kind of at odds with video art which is very hard for people to see because of the way that the art market functions.”.

According to recent reports, that said, video art has been a major inspiration for artists working in internet cinema. Arthur Jafa’s Love Is the Message, the Message Is Death (2016) in particular is often cited as a kind of totem of legitimacy for internet cinema. The film is a montage of civil rights–era footage and grainy videos of Black Americans circulated online: reaction memes, women twerking, women getting slammed to the ground by police, men getting shot by police, arms raised in the air. It’s profound love and profound despair, but also a comment on how images of Black people circulate online. When I first saw it, I was struck by how internet it felt: the video was playing on a laptop, which had been filmed by a phone camera. Of course, it turned out I’d been watching a bootleg, and that extra frame wasn’t part of the original.

Dawud’s film Palcorecore (2024) can be read in Jafa’s lineage. Like Jafa, Dawud cuts together found footage in an act of memory, love, and grief. The footage indicates Palestinians flying kites, breakdancing, rapping, riding horses, and playing by the sea. Children surround a tank; a mute man desperately mimes a murder he witnessed. “The internet exists to document its own martyrdom,” a computerized voice says, playing on the fact that the Arabic word for martyr comes from the root meaning “to witness.” “We are martyrs together,” the voice says: we are witnesses together.“What interests me about internet cinema is that it creates a history of internet artists, the thoughts and languages they develop online, and the possibility of establishing a continuity between what they produce on the internet and how it can be given a temporal form through cinema,” wrote Dawud in an email. “Internet cinema doesn’t merely document an existing culture; it participates in the creation of its history. It is a way for the internet to historicize itself.”Ultimately, internet cinema is less a practice than a name: one that gives form to a whole range of ways of making online that are often lost in the tumult of the internet’s incessant production. If there is one thing that separates the art world from online cultural production, it is that the art world is nothing if not a form of memory. In its obsession with provenance, catalogues, and archives, it is a network of stewardship. Internet cinema is a means of making an object of what is so fleeting online, by turning the internet into a film.

Biscuit-tin lids, horse brasses and scrap metal form sculptural V&A Christmas tree by Burberry

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography courtesy of Burberry.

Fashion brand Burberry‘s chief creative officer Daniel Lee worked with artist Ann Carrington to create a Christmas tree sculpture for the Victoria & Albert Museum, made from “memories, traditions and little treasures.”.

The 16-foot (4.8-metre) tree, which was unveiled this week, sits in the entrance hall of the Victoria & Albert Museum (VA’s) South Kensington location and was designed to celebrate craft and creativity.

It has been revealed that “This collaboration with Ann is a celebration of creativity and what better place to showcase this than the V&A?” Lee stated. “It’s one of my favourite museums and a constant source of inspiration to me.”.

Lee and Carrington made the tree from old money boxes, biscuit and sweet-tin lids, trinket dishes, silver trays, horse brasses and embossed plates, which were turned into rosettes and ribbons and attached to a metal frame.

The tree, which was made as part of Burberry‘s 170th anniversary celebrations, also features ribbons and bows made of scrap metal.

According to Lee, he and Carrington made the sculpture from “memories, traditions and little treasures. Objects and materials that most people would overlook.”.

Carrington added that the design was inspired by the ritual of getting old Christmas decorations out of storage in time for the festive season.

“We wanted to capture that magical moment when you retrieve the battered old box of Christmas decorations from the loft, sift through the faded party bows and tattered tinsel accumulated through the generations and begin the joyful ritual of dressing the tree,” she said.

“I’m always drawn to work that’s handmade, and Ann is a master of her craft,” Lee mentioned of the collaboration.

As well as the tree, the V&A will also be showing The Burberry Trench: Crafting an Icon, a display that traces the history of the trench coat. Burberry has a multi-year partnership with the museum and is set to open The Burberry Gallery at the South Kensington location in 2028.

Lee has previously unveiled an archive-inspired logo for Burberry, and a few years ago, the brand revealed its redesigned London flagship store.

Photography courtesy of Burberry.

#126744. This optical illusion has stumped scientists for decades, and things just got weirder

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (576 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Creativebloq ↗ Open Full Page

This optical illusion has stumped scientists for decades, and things just got weirder

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (576 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Creativebloq

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We love a good optical illusion, and we've seen plenty of mind-benders over the years, but there's one really famous one that continues to intrigue scientists.
  • A lot of people see it that way, but some people don't.
  • This optical illusion was named after Franz Carl Müller-Lyer, its creator.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We love a good optical illusion, and we've seen plenty of mind-benders over the years, but there's one really famous one that continues to intrigue scientists. The Müller-Lyer illusion looks so simple: two lines, one with arrows pointing inwards from the ends and one with arrows pointing out. One looks longer than the other, right?

A lot of people see it that way, but some people don't. Some people can immediately tell that the two horizontal lines are actually the same length (see below if you don't believe me). But the reason for this difference in perfection continues to be a topic of major debate.

This optical illusion was named after Franz Carl Müller-Lyer, its creator. Many people initially assume that the line with the arrows pointing inwards is longer than the other. But then research published in the 1960s claimed that people in African and Southeast Asian countries weren't so often fooled by the illusion. It seemed that WEIRD people were mode susceptible – that is, people whose backgrounds were Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich and from a Democracy.

That led to a theory that the apparent difference might have something to do with people in industrialised societies being more exposed to sharp angles and straight lines when growing up, and that this somehow moulds their perception.

The problem is that the suggested difference in perception has now been called into question. As reported by Sciencing, Dorsa Amir and Chaz Firestone, anthropologists at Duke and John Hopkins, have gathered evidence opposing the theory developed in the 1960s and published their findings in the Psychological Review.

They note that many variation of the Müller-Lyer illusion have been developed, including ones that work in a similar way despite using curved lines instead of straight ones. Other similar illusions abound, including the Ebbinghaus illusion, in which two identical dots are perceived to be different sizes depending on whether they're surrounded by six large dots or eight small dots. In that case, there are no lines or angles at all.

Amir and Firestone also turned up flaws in the case studies from the 1960s, and found that later reports had misconstrued the original findings. The evidence that Africans and Asians aren't fooled by the Müller-Lyer illusion appeared to be very scant.

But one discovery would seem to be even more conclusive in disproving the old WEIRD theory. The optical illusion has been tested on people who were born blind and later had lens replacement surgery, and it appears to trick people immediately after they gain sight despite them not having grown up seeing lines and angles around them.

With the WEIRD theory ruled out, it seems then that this old optical illusion has become weirder, becoming a mystery again.

At the off-peak Avios rate of **34,000 points one-way**, you're extracting **7.4 to 14.7 cents per point** — a figure that puts this redemption in a completely different category from most loyalty redemptions, where 1–2 cents per point is considered standard. To put that in human terms: if you transferred 34,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards points to Iberia Plus and used them for this booking, you'd be getting a value equivalent to someone handing you a $2,500–$5,000 check in exchange for points that cost you roughly $340–$510 in credit card spend to earn (at a 1% earn baseline). That's not a deal. That's a pricing inefficiency, and it's one that's been hiding in plain sight for travelers who only know British Airways Avios and never discovered Iberia's **separate, more generous award chart**. The FI mindset is about finding asymmetries — places where the value you receive is wildly disproportionate to what you give up. This is one of the cleanest examples in the entire travel rewards ecosystem. You're not gaming anything. You're simply using Iberia's published off-peak pricing to access a premium cabin product that most people assume is out of reach. Your future self, lying flat at 38,000 feet somewhere over the Atlantic, will be glad you learned this system.

Recent findings suggest that most people who've been in the travel rewards world for a while know about British Airways Avios.
